Dated January 1, 1968, this CIA document gives the location of work camps for Vietnamese prisoners near Nam Dinh. Nam Dinh sits in North Vietnam, and the camps held prisoners put to labor during the war. The entry is the first item in its file, which suggests a short field report rather than a long study.

Forced labor camps were part of how North Vietnam used its prisoners, and knowing where they stood mattered to American planners. A map of camp locations could guide rescue thinking, bombing choices, and talks about prisoner treatment. The document preserves the agency's picture of the camps as its sources reported them in early 1968.
cia-0000124314: Dated July 1951, this CIA document covers American prisoners of war in Shanghai. Captured Americans passed through China's great port city on their way inland during the Korean War. The paper records what the agency knew of men held so far from the fighting. Shanghai held foreign residents, journalists, and consulates longer than most Chinese cities, which made prisoner sightings there more likely to reach the agency in detail.
cia-0000132414: New plans by the Castro government are the subject of item 13 in the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated November 2, 1959. Its headline breaks off just after the words set up new, leaving the object unnamed. New bodies, new militias, or new offices could each fit the gap. The short item reports what the government was preparing, whatever the missing word was.
cia-0000132514: Cuba seeking support from Ecuador fills a CIA item dated April 1, 1961. A second Cuban topic follows in the headline but is cut short in the record title. The invasion at the Bay of Pigs was only days away at that point. Havana needed every friend it could still find. The short item tracks the courtship of Quito as analysts recorded it.
cia-0000132614: Argentina worrying over Cuban links with the Peronistas fills item 10 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated July 1, 1960. Its headline misspells the country as Agentina, a slip kept from the original. Buenos Aires feared Havana's influence over the exiled Peronist movement. The short item reports that concern and its sources.
cia-0000135814: A second meeting under the K-Program fills a CIA paper dated April 5, 1954. The paper is marked operational, and its specific subject was deleted before release. An attachment rides with the meeting record. Code names like K-Program hid the moving parts of the Guatemala campaign from plain view. The short paper keeps the meeting record in its filed form.
cia-0000136214: 1 May 1954 is the date on a declassified CIA cable about Instructions 1 on currency reform, guidance for LANGEVIN on the money of a future government. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. The file rewards slow reading, since its short heading is often the only summary the agency ever gave it.
cia-0000136314: Fighter aircraft parts top LINCOLN's list of most urgent needs in this June 1954 PBSUCCESS cable. The station asks for ten F-47 tires and tubes plus main gear tires, noting aircraft grounded at two locations for lack of them, and requests air delivery capacity from Washington. It also wants maintenance personnel sent at once to work on CALLIGERIS's aircraft, suggesting specially selected men sworn to secrecy. Logistics, here, is the operation's weak point.
cia-0000137314: Cuba dominates the briefing for the 427th National Security Council meeting. The meeting sat on 16 December 1959. Che Guevara returned in September from a long trip. He visited nine Afro-Asian countries and Yugoslavia. Foreign Minister Raul Roa spoke at the UN that month. Cuba sees the American and Soviet systems as twin evils, he said. It would ally with underdeveloped nations. Roa plans a January trip to Cairo. A high-level economic mission may follow. Egypt's ambassador backed inviting Raul Castro.
cia-0000137014: Requests for aid should go to Washington, not through Bannister to the group, headquarters urges the Guatemala City station in this July 1954 cable. It knows the station will follow up on attacks; the station should also advise whether press reports that communists escaped from embassies are true, and report on other embassies. Bannister, CALLIGERIS, and the ambassador should all receive details and guidance, since at this stage any matter CALLIGERIS raises involves policy directly or indirectly. The new regime's needs were already Washington's business.
un-ga-res-a-69-14:
Joint work between the United Nations and the world's chemical arms watchdog is the subject of Resolution A/69/14, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. It recalls the 2012 vote on ties with the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the body that polices the ban on poison arms. The Assembly had the watchdog's yearly report for 2012 and a draft report for 2013 before it.

The text takes note of both reports, sent by the watchdog's chief. It welcomes the strong joint work of the two bodies. Proof of that work, it says, was the joint UN and watchdog mission that ended Syria's declared chemical arms work, closed on 30 September 2014.
un-ga-res-114:
War in the Caucasus drove hundreds of thousands from their homes in the early 1990s, and Resolution 48/114 of the General Assembly answered on 20 December 1993. Its subject is emergency aid for refugees and displaced people in Azerbaijan. The Assembly had read the report of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, whose office works with aid and growth agencies to find lasting fixes for the uprooted.

Grave concern runs through the text at the worsening state of life in Azerbaijan, as crowds of civilians lost their homes. The Assembly welcomes the work of the UN's stopgap office and the refugee agency in the land. Both were gauging needs on the ground and steering aid to the people who needed it most.
un-ga-res-es-10-14:
Israeli acts in held East Jerusalem and the rest of the held Palestinian land fill Resolution ES-10/14, from the Assembly's tenth emergency special session. The text on file is dated 21 October 2003, in the heat of the second intifada. It recalls a long list of Security Council votes on the conflict, back to 1967. It states again that land may not be taken by force, and backs a two-state peace.

All acts of violence, terror, and destruction are condemned. Suicide bombings against Israeli civilians draw a sharp rebuke of their own. The vote belongs to the fight over the barrier Israel was then building through the West Bank, parts of which the world court would rule unlawful the next year. The catalog year of 1949 is wrong.
un-ga-res-14:
Sound money rules for a world body were laid down in Resolution 14 of the General Assembly, from the UN's first years. The lasting budget and finance setup, it says, must foster lean and cheap rule and win the trust of member states. Plans rest on the work of the Preparatory Commission and on stopgap finance rules. Those rules cover how budgets are drawn, how funds are raised and held, how spending is checked, and how the books are audited.

To help the Assembly weigh money questions, an Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions is to be named. Its nine members, up from the seven first planned, would study the budget laid before the Assembly by the Secretary-General and report on it. That body still vets every UN budget today.
un-ga-res-3314:
What counts as aggression? After years of work, the General Assembly gave the world its answer in Resolution 3314, adopted in 1974. A special team had spent seven sessions on the question, from 1967 on. Its draft Definition of Aggression, agreed by all on the team, came before the Assembly in 1974 with a plea for adoption.

The Assembly approves the definition, annexed to the vote. All states are called to shun all acts of aggression and other uses of force that breach the Charter. The text lists the acts that count: invasion, attack, blockade, and the sending of armed bands among them. Lawyers still cite the list when charges of aggression are weighed.
un-sc-res-1314: Preserved as Resolution 1314, this Security Council text carries a 1999 date in the catalog record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1514: Filed as Resolution 1514, this 2003 Security Council decision comes to the collection through a Wikisource transcription of the UN record. The Council guards world peace by voting texts like this one, and member states are expected to comply. The document's own words, arranged as recitals and numbered decisions, are the substance readers get.
un-sc-res-1614: Resolution 1614 is one of the Security Council's numbered acts, held here as an English Wikisource transcription of the official record. The Council's five permanent members shape every such text, since any of them can block it. What emerged from that process is preserved whole: findings, decisions, and the standard closing request for reports.
un-sc-res-1714: In 2006 the Council recorded Resolution 1714, and this collection keeps the record text through English Wikisource. A reader gets the institution in its working clothes: no speeches, no commentary, only the agreed findings and the voted response. That plainness is deliberate, and preserving it is the purpose served by entries like this one.
cia-0000135714: The catalog dates this Spanish-language 2506 Brigade document to 6 March 1961 and marks the date as estimated. March 1961 was the brigade's final month of preparation before the Bay of Pigs landing. An estimated date means the agency's reviewers placed the item in time rather than reading a date off it. No subject is recorded. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, its timing approximate and its contents unstated in the record.
cia-0000136614: Dated 4 January 1961, this document in Spanish is one of several 2506 Brigade records bearing that date. Brigade 2506 was made up of Cuban exiles trained and armed by the CIA for the Bay of Pigs landing. The catalog record states no subject for the item. It survives in the original Spanish in the declassified release, identified by date and collection, with its contents left to the text itself.
cia-0000136714: This Spanish-language document from the 2506 Brigade files carries an estimated date of 5 January 1960, earlier than the brigade's formation period and flagged as an estimate in the catalog. An earlier summary spoke of stakes, teamwork, and a watched enemy; none of that is in the record, and it is dropped. What stands is a Spanish brigade document with an estimated, unusually early date, released in the CIA's declassified files.
plos-pone-0000014:
Lili Yu, Valter Tucci, Shuji Kishi, and co-authors made zebrafish into a model for the aging mind in a 2006 paper. Zebrafish are small, cheap to keep, and share much of their basic brain biology with humans. The team asked whether old fish show the same slide in learning and memory that marks cognitive aging in people.

They tested fish across ages on learning tasks, looking for decline that mirrors human patterns. A fish model that ages mentally like we do would speed up research: drugs and genes could be screened in months, not decades. The study lays the groundwork, showing what changes with age in the zebrafish brain and how to measure it.
un-sc-res-1414:
Security Council Resolution 1414, adopted on May 23, 2002, recommended Timor-Leste for membership in the United Nations. The catalog year, which repeats the number 1414, predates the UN and is wrong. The small Southeast Asian land had just marked its formal independence four days earlier, after centuries of Portuguese rule, years of Indonesian control, and a UN-led transition.

Council members welcomed the new state's pledge to uphold the UN Charter, and the General Assembly seated it that September as the 191st member. The resolution capped a long struggle that had drawn UN peacekeepers and worldwide attention. For Timor-Leste, the vote turned hard-won freedom into a seat among nations.
shaftesbury-second-characters-1914:
Anthony Ashley Cooper, third Earl of Shaftesbury, left these writings on art at his death in 1713, and they stayed in draft for two centuries. Benjamin Rand edited them as Second Characters in 1914, a sequel in spirit to Shaftesbury's famed Characteristics. The subtitle, The Language of Forms, names his theme: how shapes speak.

Treatises and notes take up painting, sculpture, gardens, buildings, and the rules of taste. Shaftesbury held that beauty and moral sense spring from one root, and that good art shows order the mind can feel. His remarks helped set the terms for British writing on art through the 1700s and still reward slow reading.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d14: Crossing with Roosevelt's own note of the same date, Churchill's message to the president of June 28, 1943 is Document 14 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two letters passing each other in a single day was normal for these two leaders in wartime. The catalog record gives no topic for this one. It is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the papers that carried the alliance from summer argument to autumn agreement.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d114: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on November 10, 1943, and the message is Document 114 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. It reached Washington as the president prepared to sail, and it belongs to the last exchange of letters before the leaders met in person. The record names the date and the two men only. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series, closing the long written courtship of Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d214:
Prime Minister Churchill sent President Roosevelt telegram number 503 from London on 12 November 1943. Marked personal and most secret, it answers Roosevelt's message 417 of 10 November. That message had asked for Indian help in building four air bases for long-range bombers bound for the war against Japan.

Churchill's whole reply is one sentence of action. He says he has immediately telegraphed General Auchinleck, the commander in India, to render every possible assistance in the construction of the four bases. The short cable shows the Chengtu bomber plan moving from proposal to orders within two days.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d314:
Admiral William Leahy, the President's chief of staff, sent Roosevelt a memorandum at Cairo on 25 November 1943 on the effect of north Burma operations on cargo delivery to China. It feeds the running dispute between Lord Mountbatten and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek over airlift tonnage.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d414:
Steve Early, the President's secretary, telegraphed Harry Hopkins from Washington on 4 December 1943 about the Moscow radio leak of the Tehran Conference. Sent for Hopkins with the traveling party, the message urges the fastest possible answer in print.

All press and radio here, Early writes, headline reports received through London. The reports say Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin met at Tehran a few days ago. They discussed the war against Germany and political questions. Their conferences have now concluded, and a detailed statement is expected at any moment. The reports come from government-controlled Moscow radio, and they further complicate the mess left by Reuters' premature disclosures about the Cairo Conference. If it can mechanically be done, Early urges the quickest possible release and publication of the Tehran communiqué.

frus-1944-quebec-d14:

frus-1944-quebec-d114:

Its subject was machinery for coordinating the military efforts of the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union. arxiv-2606-05214: Analytic number theory often needs averages of special functions called Bessel moments, and umbral calculus offers a fresh way to compute them. arxiv-2606-05914: Running a computing center for particle physics means scheduling millions of jobs — and every scheduler needs realistic test data. arxiv-2606-06114: AI systems that evolve themselves — rewriting their own code and goals — could drift somewhere unhealthy. arxiv-2606-06214: AI-generated code often works but reads terribly — a maintenance nightmare. arxiv-2606-06414: The proton's structure function F2 encodes how its quarks share momentum — measured in decades of collider experiments. arxiv-2606-06614: Personalized AI often optimizes engagement — keeping you hooked — rather than serving you.
