Terao, Watanabe, Yagi and colleagues tested moving eyes and color in PLOS ONE in 2010. When eyes smoothly follow a moving target, vision does not simply blur. The team asked whether that smooth pursuit changes how finely people can judge color changes over time.

Pursuit eye movements improved the time resolution of color perception in their tests. Motion and color, long studied apart, turn out to interact. That interplay matters for basic vision science. It also informs display design, where screens must match how the eye truly samples a moving colored world.
plos-pone-0011314:
Hurt, Torrone, Green and colleagues tracked drug use and HIV in North Carolina for PLOS ONE in 2010. They studied young men newly diagnosed with HIV between 2000 and 2005. Records let them measure how many reported methamphetamine use around the time of diagnosis.

Stimulant use shadowed a notable share of new cases in this group. That behavioral overlap points to where prevention can do most good. Programs that address drug use and sexual risk together may reach these young men better than separate efforts. The study gives HIV prevention a defined, at risk population in the state.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1214:
Hurley in China addressed this message to the President and the Secretary of State on 20 July 1945. A dispatch aimed at the very top marks the weight its writer gave it. Hurley's post stood at the center of the China tangle, where war with Japan mixed with a looming civil clash.

American policy sought to hold China together as an ally and a future great power. Hurley reported on that effort to the two men who owned the policy. This message carried his word to the summit level. It shows how far the Potsdam web reached: a cable from China landing on the president's desk in Germany.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1314:
Prime Minister Attlee wrote to President Truman on 1 August 1945, the summit's last full day. Attlee had led the British team for less than a week. His note to the president belongs to the closing business of the conference.

By then Britain's new government had taken the talks' reins in full. The final protocol was being readied for signing, and the leaders' own channels carried the last courtesies and confirmations. This message is Attlee's word in that closing set. It shows the new prime minister ending the summit as a partner in his own right, no longer in Churchill's shadow.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1414:
A memorandum of conversation dated 23 August 1945 records a talk held after the Potsdam Conference and after the war's end. Such memoranda were written by an officer who sat in, to fix what was said. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Memoranda of conversation are the nearest thing to transcripts that diplomacy keeps. They note who met, what each side said, and what was left open. Readers prize them because spoken words, unlike cables, can be denied later unless a paper like this one pins them down. Placed near the volume's end, this record shows the conference's business still being talked through weeks after the leaders went home.
frus-1945-50-intel-d14:
Executive Order 9621, signed by President Truman on 20 September 1945, is one of the landmark papers in the volume. By it, the Office of Strategic Services ceased to exist. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

The order split the OSS in two. Its research and analysis branch went to the State Department. The rest went to the War Department as a leftover unit. With one signature, the wartime spy service Donovan had built was gone, and the fight over its heirs began in earnest. Readers will find nearly every later paper in the volume living in this order's shadow. It is the hinge on which the whole collection turns.
frus-1945-50-intel-d114:
A memorandum by Wright, the director of central intelligence's executive officer, is dated 11 July 1946. Executive officers turn a director's wishes into the staff's orders. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Wright's paper belongs to the CIG's build-out under Vandenberg, when the group was hiring, drafting charters, and claiming missions at speed. An executive's memorandum shows the director's office thinking on paper: priorities listed, tasks assigned, arguments framed. Readers interested in how a small coordinating staff became an agency will find these staff papers essential. The famous letters between chiefs decided the questions; papers like this one made the decisions run.
frus-1945-50-intel-d214:
Dated 14 May 1947, this memorandum runs from the National Intelligence Authority to the Director of Central Intelligence (Hillenkoetter). It is document 214 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d314:
A memorandum dated 13 October 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination, Central Intelligence Agency (Wisner). The reader was Joseph A. Frank of the Office of Policy Coordination. The State Department prints it as document 314 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d414:
Director of Central Intelligence Roscoe Hillenkoetter wrote to the Army's director of intelligence, Irwin, on 15 February 1950. The memo is document 414 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Army intelligence was older, larger, and proud of its own record. The CIA director had to coordinate it without owning it, a hard task set by law. A direct memo between the two chiefs shows that uneasy partnership at work in the third year of the agency's life. The Army guarded its own secrets hard, so each such memo was a small act of trust.
frus-1861-d14:
Norman Judd wrote from Berlin to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 July 1861. The dispatch is document 14 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Three days earlier, Union troops had been beaten at Bull Run in Virginia. News of that scale crossed the ocean slowly, and posts abroad braced for its effect. Judd's late July letter belongs to the uneasy weeks when Europe asked whether the Union could last. Judd's standing with Lincoln gave his reports a weight beyond his post's small size. News from home reached him by the same slow mails he used to answer it.
frus-1861-d114:
Chevalier Hülsemann, the Austrian envoy in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 August 1861. The letter is document 114 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Hülsemann was a veteran of a famous clash with Washington a decade earlier. Austria watched the American war from a cool distance. His August letter brings the voice of the Vienna court into the record, through its careful envoy at the capital. Hülsemann's earlier clash with Washington, in 1850, had made his name known across America. A known name in Washington cut both ways, and Hülsemann wore his with care.
frus-1861-d214:
In a report dated 10 June 1861, Mr. Dillon wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It was printed as Document 214 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The letter comes from the opening months of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d14:
In a letter dated 5 February 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 14 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the winter of the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d114:
One more voice from abroad reached Washington on 31 July 1862: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London writing to Seward. It was printed as Document 114 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d214: Dated 30 May 1862 and addressed to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, a letter from a Mr. Edwards survives as Document 214 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume, filed among the British papers. The record gives no first name or post for Edwards. So the entry rests on its date, its reader, and its place in the legation file.
frus-1862-d314:
Four Seward dispatches to Paris bear the date 24 September 1862, and the first is Document 314 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All four went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

The cluster went out two days after the Emancipation Proclamation was announced, the busiest diplomatic moment of the fall. Washington had much to send: the proclamation itself, the war news, and fresh guidance. This first letter of the set opens a batch that shows the Department working at its highest tempo of the year. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year.
frus-1862-d414:
Horace J. Perry, secretary of the American legation in Madrid, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 December 1861. It is Document 414 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Perry closed the year 1861 in Madrid as the legation's working hand, reporting between ministers. Spain had troops landing in Mexico that month, and Cuba lay close to the seat of war. His year-end report gave Washington a view of Spanish plans and temper at a moment when the Trent affair had just strained ties with Britain. Such reports let Seward judge which European courts might still be kept friendly or at least quiet.
frus-1862-d514:
James Shepherd Pike wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from The Hague on 13 August 1862. His report is Document 514 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress. Its heading keeps the punctuation as it stands in the volume.

Mid-August 1862 found the Union calling for more men and Europe debating whether the war could ever end. Pike's reading of Dutch opinion in that debate was useful precisely because the Netherlands had little at stake but trade. His reports also handled the post's steady small business. The letter is one of the densest month's entries in the Hague file. It shows how much wartime work had accumulated at even the quieter posts. That work had piled up by the war's second summer.
frus-1862-d614:
On 10 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Bradford R. Wood, the American minister in Denmark. The instruction is Document 614 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

February's Union victories gave Seward material to send his ministers, and the Danish order carried it to Copenhagen. Denmark watched the war from a trading nation's distance, with its own German question absorbing its court. Wood's task was to keep the American cause correctly understood there and to handle the maritime business that arose between the two states. The dispatch is one of the early-year orders by which Seward set all his northern posts to the same work in the same weeks.
frus-1862-d714:
Five days after Molina's letter reached him, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote back, on 24 September 1862. Molina was Costa Rica's envoy in Washington. The reply is document 714 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Quick answers kept foreign envoys in good humor and their business moving. Seward's reply to Molina is one turn in a brisk exchange that ran through the fall of 1862. The two men's letters dealt with the ties between the United States and Costa Rica. Washington had little thought to spare for small lands, yet it gave some. That courtesy, on paper, is part of the record.
frus-1863p1-d14:
William H. Seward addressed this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 15 December 1862. Adams held the London legation, the post Washington watched most closely. The letter is document 14 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mid-December letters from Washington carried the government's line after a hard autumn of war. Seward had to tell Adams how to meet British feelers about peace talks without giving ground on the Union's cause. This letter is part of that guidance. It shows the secretary at his desk work: short sheets, sent by each steamer, that kept one envoy aimed at one great aim.
frus-1863p1-d114:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 11 March 1863 to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 114 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The middle sheet of a three-letter day took its own head of the brief, as was Seward's habit all through this file. Adams dealt with the British foreign office week by week, and each sheet armed him for a point. This letter is the second of the 11 March set. With its mates, it shows Washington feeding its envoy in the tight loop the sea mail allowed.
frus-1863p1-d214:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 17 June 1863. It appears as document 214 of the 1863 papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built near Liverpool, had slipped away in 1862 and was raiding Union trade. Washington pressed London to stop such ships and answer for the losses. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d314:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Gideon Welles, the Secretary of the Navy, on 31 October 1862. The letter is document 314 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers.

Foreign complaints about the Union navy landed on Seward's desk, while the ships themselves answered to Welles. Letters between the two secretaries sorted out which captures to defend, which to explain, and which to regret. Blockade seizures of British vessels were the sorest point between Washington and London. This internal note shows the machinery behind the polished answers sent to the British legation.
frus-1863p1-d414:
One entry in the running Washington exchange, this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, is dated 9 March 1863. It stands as document 414 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Read together, these letters trace a slow cooling of the crisis mood of 1861 and 1862. Recognition of the South grew less likely with each month the channel stayed open. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d514:
15 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d614:
William Stuart took up his pen on 17 August 1863 and wrote to William H. Seward. Stuart was Britain's chargé d'affaires in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Letters like this one were the tools of a quiet contest. The Union meant to keep Britain out of the war, and it made that case note by note. British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020014:
Christiane Landgraf, Simona Panni, Luisa Montecchi-Palazzi, and others presented a protein mapping method in PLOS Biology in 2004. Many proteins link up through short stretches that fit into small pockets on partner proteins. The team scanned whole sets of proteins with short peptides to find those links.

Each scan tests huge numbers of pairs at once, far more than one-by-one lab work allows. The result is a network map of which proteins can touch which. Such maps help predict how signals travel through a cell and where a fault might cause disease. They also give drug makers a list of contacts that a well aimed compound might block or boost.
plos-pone-0000114:
Elin Lehrmann, Carlo Colantuoni, Amy Deep-Soboslay, and colleagues published this brain study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It asks whether cocaine, cannabis, and phencyclidine, three very different drugs of abuse, leave a shared mark on the human brain. The team looked for gene activity changes common to all three.

A central goal of addiction research is finding brain changes shared across drugs, since those may drive dependence itself. The authors compare transcription patterns linked to each drug and pull out the overlap. Work like this points drug research toward the common machinery of addiction rather than the quirks of one substance.
plos-pone-0000214:
Pekka Janhunen, Hermanni Kaartokallio, Ilona Oksanen, and colleagues published this Earth history paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It concerns the Neoproterozoic icehouse, a time hundreds of millions of years ago when ice may have covered much of the planet. The authors argue biological feedbacks both caused and ended that deep freeze.

The paper also looks ahead: cold conditions may carry astrobiological lessons, including prospects for faster evolution. The authors link microbial life, climate, and planetary change in one loop. Their argument treats the snowball Earth episode not just as a climate event but as a turning point for life itself.
plos-pone-0000314:
Kevin C. Leonard, Dino Petrin, Stuart G. Coupland, and colleagues published this eye research paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited disease that kills photoreceptors, the light-sensing cells of the retina, causing blindness. The authors study XIAP, a protein that blocks cell death, and its protection of photoreceptors in animal models of the disease.

Slowing photoreceptor death could preserve sight even without fixing the faulty gene. The authors test whether boosting this natural brake on cell death saves the cells. The work supports gene therapy approaches that deliver protective proteins to the retina.
plos-pone-0000414:
Yanling Zhang and colleagues studied a protein that helps kidney cells keep their shape and tiny hair-like sensors, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, collectrin, is a target of the gene regulator HNF-1β. The team examined collecting duct cells, which line the kidney's final urine-handling tubes.

They focused on collectrin's role in maintaining primary cilia and cell polarity. A primary cilium is the single antenna-like hair most cells carry. Cell polarity is the cell's sense of top and bottom. When cilia or polarity fail, kidney cysts and other defects can follow. The work links a diabetes-related regulator to the basic architecture of kidney cells.
plos-pone-0000514:
Nadia A. Ayoub and colleagues read the full genes behind spider silk, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dragline silk, the spider's lifeline and web frame, outperforms most human-made fibers for its weight. The team produced the blueprint for this high-performance biomaterial: full-length spider dragline silk genes, which are enormous and repetitive and had resisted complete sequencing.

The repeat structure is exactly what makes silk strong and elastic, and exactly what made the genes hard to read. Full sequences let engineers copy the design into microbes or materials with the proportions right. Biomaterials work of this kind aims to manufacture silk's properties without farming spiders.
plos-pone-0000614:
Peter R. Teske, Isabelle Papadopoulos, Christopher D. McQuaid and colleagues turned to a very old fashion question in PLOS ONE in 2007. Shell beads made from the southern African tick shell are the earliest known ornaments worn by humans. Beads from about 75,000 years ago, found in a cave on South Africa's south coast, were larger than later ones.

Three explanations compete in the title itself: climate change, genetics, or human choice. The authors compare Pleistocene shells with Holocene ones to weigh why the size shifted. A change in taste would say something about early human culture. A change in climate or genes would point to the shells' own biology instead.
plos-pone-0000714:
Yale J. Passamaneck, Anna-Katerina Hadjantonakis and Anna Di Gregorio filmed muscle cells building a sea squirt's tail, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Axial elongation, growth along the body's length, shapes developing organisms. In the ascidian Ciona intestinalis, the larva's tail extends in a striking example of this process. Muscle cells set along the tail's sides elongate and differentiate on their own schedule.

The team describes dynamic, polarized behaviors in those cells as the tail forms. Polarized means the cells have distinct fronts and backs guiding their movement and shape. Such cell-level detail explains how a simple larva builds a working swimming tail so quickly and reliably.
plos-pone-0000814:
Qi Wang and Christopher Lee worked on a trap in the study of how proteins change, using HIV as their case. Scientists often infer that two sites in a protein work together when they change together over time. But shared ancestry can fake that pattern. Sites can look linked just because they were inherited in the same viral line, a problem classed as background linkage disequilibrium.

Their study sorts true linked change from that background effect. The test proteins were HIV protease and reverse transcriptase, the two enzymes most HIV drugs target. The stakes are practical: falsely linked sites can mislead work on how the virus escapes drugs. A cleaner method points drug design at real weak spots.
plos-pone-0000914:
Ana-Belen Martin-Cuadrado, Purificacion Lopez-Garcia, Juan-Carlos Alba and co-authors sampled the gene pool of the deep Mediterranean Sea, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Metagenomics reads DNA straight from the environment, revealing microbes that never grow in a lab. Most sea studies of this kind had focused on sunlit surface waters.

The deep Mediterranean is different: a warm bathypelagic habitat, far below the light. Reading its microbes shows what life does where food is scarce and pressure is high. Work of this sort keeps rewriting basic ideas in microbial ecology. It shows how much of the living world stays hidden until its DNA is read directly.
plos-pone-0001014:
Tina Rich and Archana Varadaraj tested how fusion partners change the harm done by a repeated protein stretch, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Clumps of protein inside the nucleus mark several folding diseases. Much of what we know comes from glowing fusion proteins carrying polyglutamine repeats, the same repeats behind Huntington's disease.

Ataxin-1 is one such protein. The pair ask whether the partner fused to it changes how lethal the repeat is and how it aggregates. If partners change the outcome, then lab results depend on the test construct, not just the repeat. That caution matters for every study built on fusion proteins.
plos-pone-0001114:
Nearly a fifth of human cancers around the world are linked to infections, Xing Guo Wang and co-authors note in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their examples include liver cancer tied to hepatitis B and C viruses, and cervical cancer tied to human papilloma virus. The authors argue that these virus-linked tumors need fresh lines of attack.

Rather than treating such cancers only as growths to cut or poison, the authors propose a different target. They would go after the viral proteins, called antigens, that sit inside the tumor cells. Those antigens could serve as targets for new treatments. The same targets might also help prevent tumors of viral origin before they form.
plos-pone-0001214:
Cell-mediated immunity is needed to stop HIV spreading from cell to cell, and killer T cell responses are central to it. Ammar Achour and colleagues tested an unusual vaccine candidate in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The candidate is a synthetic peptide called B1, built by mathematical transformation of HIV protein structures rather than copied from them.

The peptide shares no sequence homology with HIV, yet earlier work hinted it could still provoke immunity. The authors report HIV-1 envelope-specific cell-mediated immunity induced by this non-homologous peptide. If it holds up, the design route behind B1 could widen the search for vaccine parts.
plos-pone-0001314:
Epigenetic changes, especially DNA methylation, are among the earliest abnormalities in tumor formation. Jared Ordway and colleagues searched breast cancer for methylation changes that occur at high frequency, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Cytosine methylation is thermodynamically stable, which makes it attractive as a biomarker that can survive in clinical samples.

The authors report identification of novel high-frequency DNA methylation changes in breast cancer. Changes present in most tumors are the most useful for detection tests. Their catalogue adds candidate markers for the long-running effort to catch breast cancer from a blood or tissue sample.
plos-pone-0001414:
Matthias Schaefer, Julia Steringer, and Frank Lyko wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on an enzyme in fruit flies called Dnmt2. Enzymes of this family are kept across many species, yet their true job was in doubt. This one bears all the marks of a DNA tagging enzyme. Still, tests kept pointing to a role with RNA instead.

The team found the fly enzyme bound to the scaffold inside the cell nucleus. It could reach DNA while the cell was dividing. Those facts keep both roles in play and refine where to look next. Sorting this enzyme out matters for the wider tale of how gene tags evolve.
plos-pone-0001514:
Birte Meyer and Jan Kuever wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that models an enzyme of sulfur germs. The enzyme drives a step in how some germs burn or store sulfur. It works forward in sulfate eating germs and in reverse in sulfur burning ones. No lab shape for it existed, so the pair built a model from kin enzymes.

Their model maps the enzyme's shape and its key working parts. Those parts include a flavin helper and two iron sulfur clusters. A sound model lets labs guess how mutations will shift the enzyme. It also aids study of sulfur cycles in soil and sea.
plos-pone-0001614:
Michael Bethune and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a monkey model for gluten sensitivity. In celiac disease, gluten in food sparks gut harm, poor food uptake, and loose stools. A faithful animal model had been lacking, which slowed work on the ill. The team tested whether rhesus monkeys can fill that gap.

Some monkeys did show the gut harm, blood marks, and signs seen in human celiac disease when fed gluten. That makes them a rare model that mirrors the human course. With it, labs can test diets, drugs, and the ill's first steps in a close kin. Ethical care bounds such work, which adds to its value.
plos-pone-0001714:
Karin Dedek, Chethan Pandarinath, Nazia M. Alam, and their co-authors asked how the retina adapts between night and day in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The visual system adjusts to its setting. Retinal ganglion cells, which send the eye's output to the brain, shift their spatial tuning when light changes. That shift is thought to come from changes in how horizontal cells are coupled to each other.

The team tested whether horizontal cell coupling plays a causal role in ganglion cell adaptability. The full text gives the retina preparations, the coupling measurements, and the tuning shifts. The coupling acts like a switch that reconfigures the eye's circuits for dim or bright scenes, a design that artificial vision systems also exploit.
plos-pone-0001814:
Shashank Gupta, Sabine Höpner, Bernd Rupp, and their co-authors studied how immune display molecules swap their cargo in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Class II MHC molecules display peptides on cell surfaces for surveillance by CD4 T cells. A complex processing pathway delivers only stable peptide-MHC complexes to the surface, so the display reflects the cell's contents.

The team reports that anchor side chains of short peptide fragments trigger ligand exchange of class II MHC molecules. The full text gives the binding experiments and the structural evidence. Understanding exchange rules helps vaccine designers load chosen peptides onto MHC molecules deliberately, rather than by trial and error.
plos-pone-0001914:
Naeem Ali and co-authors reported that a protein long cast as a mere holder has its own immune effects, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The protein, called latency associated peptide, binds TGF-beta1 and holds it in a latent, inactive form. Most work assumed the peptide's only job was to keep that signal locked away.

Past work had shown the peptide can make lining cells move, but effects on white blood cells were unknown. The team tested the peptide in lab dishes and in living animals, apart from TGF-beta1. They report immune effects of its own. If a holder protein also acts alone, immune models need a rewrite.
plos-pone-0002014:
Cory Toth and co-authors studied a protein that helps severed nerve fibers regrow, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Axons, the long fibers of nerve cells, regrow poorly after injury. Blame falls on both a hostile scar setting and a weak inborn drive to regrow inside the neuron. The steps of that weakness were unclear.

The team focused on Ndel1, a protein tied to how cells build their inner frame. As the title states, Ndel1 promotes axon regeneration via intermediate filaments, one class of that frame. A regrowth lever inside the cell is a hope for spinal and nerve repair.
plos-pone-0002114:
Maorong Chen and co-authors found the rings that make a major potassium channel one-way, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. BK channels are large-conductance channels opened by calcium and voltage, and they serve many tissues. Their auxiliary beta subunits add much of the channels' diversity, which is fundamental to their right function in each tissue.

The team describe a feature of the human beta two subunit's outer segment: rings rich in lysine, a charged building block. As the title states, these extracellular rings confer the outward rectification of BK channels, a bias to pass current one way. Form explains function here, residue by residue.
plos-pone-0002214:
Linea Melchior, Toomas Kivisild, Niels Lynnerup, and co-authors extracted DNA from Viking Age skeletons in Denmark, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Ancient human DNA is easily swamped by modern DNA from handlers, so results in this field have often been doubted. Strict lab rules exist to guard against such contamination.

The team's skeletons had stayed untouched by humans for about 1,000 years until careful excavation. That rare history let them argue their DNA results were authentic. Verified Viking DNA can test sagas against genetics. It traces kinship and migration in early medieval Scandinavia with a firmer hand than most ancient studies can claim.
plos-pone-0002314:
Hidehito Takayama, Prashen Chelikani, Philip Reeves, and co-authors produced and purified a human membrane protein called CD81, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Membrane proteins are prime drug targets, but studying their structure requires making large amounts in a working form, which is notoriously hard. CD81 belongs to the tetraspanin family and is also the entry receptor used by hepatitis C virus.

The team built a mammalian cell line that makes CD81 at high level under a switchable promoter, then purified it in a single affinity step. They characterized the protein to confirm it stayed functional. A clean supply of CD81 enables structural work and screens for entry blockers.
plos-pone-0002414:
Work from Addessi and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Elsa Addessi, Alessandra Mancini, Lara Crescimbene, and others. Its subject is preference Transitivity and Symbolic Representation in Capuchin Monkeys ( Cebus apella ). Can non-human animals comprehend and employ symbols?

The most convincing empirical evidence comes from language-trained apes, but little is known about this ability in monkeys. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002514:
In 2008, Lundby and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Alicia Lundby, Hiroki Mutoh, Dimitar Dimitrov, and others. Its subject is engineering of a Genetically Encodable Fluorescent Voltage Sensor Exploiting Fast Ci-VSP Voltage-Sensing Movements. Ci-VSP contains a voltage-sensing domain (VSD) homologous to that of voltage-gated potassium channels.

Using charge displacement (‘gating’ current) measurements we show that voltage-sensing movements of this VSD can occur within 1 ms in mammalian membranes. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002614:
A research team led by Pantano reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Sergio Pantano, Francesco Zonta, Fabio Mammano, and others. Its subject is a Fully Atomistic Model of the Cx32 Connexon. Connexins are plasma membrane proteins that associate in hexameric complexes to form channels named connexons.

Two connexons in neighboring cells may dock to form a “gap junction” channel, i.e. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002714:
Yoshimi Endo led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was role of sox-9, ER81 and VE-Cadherin in retinoic Acid-Mediated Trans-Differentiation of breast cancer cells. Authorship is credited in the record to Yoshimi Endo and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Many aspects of development, tumor growth and metastasis depend upon the provision of an adequate vasculature. The summary also notes a further point. This can be a result of regulated angiogenesis, recruitment of circulating endothelial progenitors and/or vascular trans-differentiation. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002814:
Joseph Alan Wamstad led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was role of the transcriptional corepressor bcor in embryonic stem cell differentiation and early embryonic development. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Joseph Alan Wamstad, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Bcor (BCL6 corepressor) is a widely expressed gene that is mutated in patients with X-linked Oculofaciocardiodental (OFCD) syndrome. The summary also notes a further point. BCOR regulates gene expression in association with a complex of proteins capable of epigenetic modification of chromatin. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002914:
Todd Harshbarger and Allen Song probed the tail end of the brain's blood signal in 2008. In fMRI scans, the BOLD signal rises with activity and then dips below baseline, a phase called the post-stimulus undershoot. That dip is perhaps the least understood part of the signal.

By adding diffusion weighting, which is sensitive to small water movement, the team tried to separate blood vessel effects from neuron effects. The PLOS ONE paper links the dip's sensitivity to a hierarchy of vessels and neurons. Scan analysts can use that to read fMRI results with more care.
plos-pone-0003014:
Vincenzo Penteriani and Maria del Mar Delgado proposed in 2008 that owls signal breeding status with droppings and prey feathers. Many animals mark key spots in their home range with materials that carry information. Visual signaling had already been shown to play a once-unrecognized role in eagle owl communication, both territorial and parental.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors argue faeces and prey feathers may signal current reproduction in these owls. That would let rivals and mates read breeding state at a site without the owner present. Field biologists get a testable reading of marks once dismissed as mere mess.
plos-pone-0003114:
Brent Bill, Darius Balciunas, Joshua McCarra and co-authors studied choroid plexus development and Notch signaling in zebrafish in 2008. The choroid plexus is an epithelial and vascular structure in the brain's ventricles and a critical part of the blood-brain barrier. It produces and regulates cerebrospinal fluid and blocks entry of harmful substances.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team sets out development of the zebrafish plexus and its requirements for Notch signaling, a core cell-to-cell pathway. Knowing the signals that build the plexus helps explain disorders where fluid balance in the brain goes wrong early in life.
plos-pone-0003214:
Yaoxing Huang, Michael Krasnitz, Raul Rabadan and colleagues describe a recoding method for an HIV DNA vaccine in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The manuscript describes a novel strategy to improve HIV DNA vaccine design. Using a new information theory based bioinformatic algorithm, the team identify a set of nucleotide motifs common in the coding region of HIV but under-represented in highly expressed genes.

The aim is a recoding method to improve the humoral immune response to the vaccine. Readers see vaccine design treated as a sequence engineering problem. Changing silent parts of the code may raise antibody output without changing the protein the immune system must learn.
plos-pone-0003314:
Jehangir S. Wadia, Monica Schaller, R. Anthony Williamson and colleagues study how the harmful prion protein enters cells in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Transmissible spongiform encephalopathies are fatal neurodegenerative disorders. They include variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans. They also include bovine spongiform encephalopathy in cattle. In these diseases, the host cellular prion protein misfolds into an infectious form.

The title reports that pathologic prion protein infects cells by lipid-raft dependent macropinocytosis, a drinking-like uptake route. Readers see prions use a bulk entry pathway rather than a single receptor. That route may suggest new points to block prion spread between cells.
plos-pone-0007414:
Joachim Lange, Marc de Lussanet, Simone Kuhlmann, and colleagues tested motion perception in people who cannot recognize faces in 2009. Prosopagnosia is a deficit in recognizing people from their faces. Congenital prosopagnosia is not caused by a brain lesion and has presumably been present since early childhood in affected people.

Face recognition might share machinery with biological motion perception, the ability to read movement of living beings. The authors test that perception in congenital prosopagnosia. They report impairments of biological motion perception. Their finding suggests the condition reaches beyond faces into wider social perception.
plos-pone-0007514:
Guillaume Jacquot and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Vpr, a multi-purpose protein of HIV-1. Vpr shows many functions in laboratory tests, but which of them matter during real infection is less clear. The team characterized Vpr variants taken from two patients. One patient's disease progressed rapidly, while the other controlled the virus for years. Two single-letter changes, Q65R and R77Q, drew their focus.

The variants behaved differently in functional tests. Those small substitutions changed what Vpr could do. That suggests the protein's fine details help shape how infection unfolds in a person. Comparing natural variants is a way to let the virus reveal its own priorities. The work connects laboratory functions to clinical courses. It may help explain why HIV progresses at such different speeds in different people.
plos-pone-0007614:
Xiao-Juan Jiang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a family of brain-wiring genes in a reptile. Protocadherins are adhesion molecules found mostly in the nervous system. They are thought to help establish the complex neural network during development. Their genes sit in a distinctive cluster in vertebrate genomes. The team identified and analyzed that whole cluster in the green anole lizard, then compared it across vertebrates.

The lizard's set fills a missing branch in the family's story. Comparing reptile, bird, and mammal clusters shows which genes were gained, lost, or kept. Adhesion molecules with many variants may give each neuron a surface identity. Evolution's handling of the cluster hints at how that identity system grew. The study is comparative genomics aimed at the wiring of brains.
plos-pone-0007714:
Gisella Puga Yung and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns Crohn's disease in children, a long-term gut inflammation. The disease is thought to arise when the immune system reacts wrongly to gut microbes. Heat shock proteins are among the targets it may attack.

The authors found that T cells react to small pieces of heat shock proteins. Those reactions add to the autoimmune inflammation in young patients. Pinpointing such targets, called epitopes, helps explain why the gut stays inflamed. It may also guide gentler treatments that calm only the harmful response.
plos-pone-0007814:
Tammy-Claire Troy and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies skin barrier failure in engineered mice. Healthy skin blocks infection, water loss, ultraviolet light and temperature swings. That barrier weakens as skin ages, for reasons not fully known.

The team altered a protein called claudin 6 in the mice's outer skin. The mutant protein lacks its tail end. The mice developed dermatitis and barrier problems like those of aging. Their skin offers a model for studying how the barrier breaks down. It may also help test creams or drugs that restore it.
plos-pone-0007914:
Irene De Biase and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It explains one layer of gene silencing in Friedreich ataxia. More than fifteen inherited diseases come from repeated DNA letters expanding. In this disease, a GAA repeat in the FXN gene grows too long in both copies.

The expanded repeat cuts the gene's transcription, starving cells of its protein. The authors link the silencing to loss of CTCF, a protein that binds DNA at a marker sequence. Antisense transcription across the region also plays a part. The findings suggest routes to switch the gene back on.
plos-pone-0008014:
Payel Bhanja and colleagues tested a gut growth factor against radiation harm in mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. Hard radiation kills the gut's lining cells and the cells that renew them. The result is diarrhea, fluid loss, infection, and often death.

The factor, R-spondin1, feeds the gut's own stem cells. Mice given it kept more of their gut lining and lived through doses that killed untreated mice. A shield built on the body's own repair crew could serve after accidents or attack, and perhaps ease cancer radiation care as well.
plos-pone-0008114:
Anfumbom Kfutwah and colleagues studied the placenta's signal mix in Cameroonian mothers with HIV and malaria in PLOS ONE in 2009. Placental cytokines, small signal proteins, keep pregnancy steady and shield the unborn child. Both infections were already suspected of stirring that mix.

In women carrying both infections, malaria measurably threw the signal mix off balance. A skewed mix can weaken the placenta's guard and harm birth outcomes. The result helps explain why mothers facing both ills fare worse, and it argues for malaria protection as part of HIV pregnancy care.
plos-pone-0008214:
Diana B. Peckys and colleagues presented a microscopy method in PLOS ONE in 2009 for imaging whole cells. Scientists need nanoscale views to see single proteins at work. They also need them to watch nanomaterials interact with living systems. The team imaged whole fixed cells while the cells sat in liquid. They used a scanning transmission electron microscope for the job.

A liquid enclosure kept the cells wet inside the microscope. That is hard, because electron microscopes normally require a vacuum. Imaging cells in a near natural state preserves fine detail. The method opens new ways to study cell structure at very small scales.
plos-pone-0008314:
Richard T. Frank and colleagues used stem cells to carry cancer drugs in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Monoclonal antibodies have become tools for cancer therapy. Their large size limits how well they penetrate solid tumors. It also blocks them from crossing into the brain. A delivery vehicle that homes to tumors could solve both problems.

Neural stem cells naturally migrate toward tumors. The team used them as a platform to deliver therapeutic antibodies. Tumor-specific delivery would concentrate treatment where it is needed. It could also reduce side effects elsewhere in the body.
plos-pone-0008414:
Nargis Nasrin and colleagues studied an enzyme partnership in cells in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. SIRT1 is a deacetylase that regulates many pathways, including stress protection. It acts on substrates such as histones, FOXOs, PGC-1 alpha, and p53. Those actions lead to cellular protection against damage. The team identified a functional interaction involving the kinase JNK1.

JNK1 phosphorylates SIRT1 and promotes its enzymatic activity. A stress kinase thus switches on a stress protector. That pairing helps cells coordinate their defense programs. It adds a control point to pathways tied to aging and survival.
plos-pone-0008514:
Joao Dias and co-authors solve a tick protein structure in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Chemokines are signals that guide inflammatory cells to tissues. They act through receptors on cell surfaces. Blocking a chemokine and its receptor can reduce inflammation. Ticks make a protein called Evasin-1 that soaks up chemokines. It keeps tick bites from provoking a strong host response. The team crystallize Evasin-1 bound to the chemokine CCL3.

Their crystal structure shows exactly how Evasin-1 sequesters CCL3. That atomic view explains its tight and selective binding. It offers a template for designing anti-inflammatory drugs. Nature's own blocker becomes a blueprint for medicine.
plos-pone-0008614:
Michael Berney and co-authors study energy flexibility in mycobacteria in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Mycobacteria are obligate aerobes that require oxygen for growth. Paradoxically, they can survive and metabolize under hypoxia, or low oxygen. The mechanisms behind this metabolic plasticity were unknown. That survival lets tuberculosis germs persist in low-oxygen lung lesions. The team report on adaptation of Mycobacterium to starvation and hypoxia together.

They find unique flexibility in energy metabolism under those stresses. The germ rewires how it generates ATP when oxygen and food are scarce. That flexibility explains its legendary persistence in hosts. It also exposes metabolic weaknesses that drugs might exploit.
plos-pone-0008714:
Patrick Ott, Anne Hamilton, Amanda Jones, and colleagues ran a phase II trial of a cancer drug. Their report appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drug, ixabepilone, steadies the cell's inner scaffolding so cancer cells cannot divide well. Lab work had hinted it might help against melanoma that has spread. Phase II trials test whether such hints hold in patients.

Patients with metastatic melanoma received the drug at several centers. The team tracked tumor shrinkage and side effects. Even a modest response can matter when few options remain. The results help decide whether bigger trials of this drug are worthwhile.
plos-pone-0008814:
Rachel Sarig, Ora Fuchs, Lilach Tencer, and colleagues tested whether committed muscle cells can change identity. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells are usually thought locked into their chosen fate. Reports of fate switching often turn out to involve cell fusion instead. Cloned myogenic cells, with known single-cell origins, offered a rigorous test. Placing them in a nerve-friendly setting posed the challenge.

Inside living hosts, the muscle clones became neuron-like cells. Careful checks ruled out fusion as the explanation. Genuine reprogramming in the body raises hopes for repair therapies. It also reopens basic questions about how fixed cell identity really is.
plos-pone-0008914:
Michael Boivin, Paul Bangirana, and Rebecca Smith compared two kinds of working memory in African schoolchildren. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Working memory holds sights and sounds briefly while the mind works. Earlier work in Congo found the two spans independent in children. American and Lao children, by contrast, showed linked spans when older. Culture and schooling may shape that link. Children in Senegal and Uganda formed the new test groups.

Tests measured visual-spatial and auditory-verbal spans side by side. How the spans related bore on universal claims about memory development. Local data keep child psychology honest about its sample base. Most classic studies draw on a narrow slice of the world's children.
plos-pone-0009014:
Coralie Spiegelhalter and co-authors joined live filming of cells with freeze-frame electron pictures, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cell biologists need both movies of living cells and fine structural detail. Light microscopes give the movies; electron microscopes give the detail. Matching the same moment across both views is technically hard.

Their method films cells, then freezes them under high pressure at a chosen instant. The frozen cells then go to electron microscopy for three-dimensional structure. Events caught live can be inspected at near-atomic neatness afterwards. The pipeline turns a passing moment in a cell's life into a lasting specimen.
plos-pone-0009114:
Bryan Clarkson, Wendy Gilbert, and Jennifer Doudna asked whether yeast's two protein-making starters can cover for each other, in PLOS ONE in 2010. eIF4G is a scaffold that gathers an RNA message for translation. It reads tags at both ends of the message to recruit the ribosome. Many eukaryotes carry several versions of this factor.

Baker's yeast has two eIF4G isoforms with partly shared duties. The team tested how much their functions overlap. Each could substitute for the other across much of the workload. Backup copies like these keep protein production running when one fails.
plos-pone-0009214:
Antoine Nougairède and colleagues published this flu surveillance report in PLOS ONE in 2010. It covers the first months of the 2009 swine flu pandemic in south-eastern France. The new virus, influenza A H1N1sw, was first detected in France in April 2009. Reference labs across the French Defence Zones ran the testing.

The authors report virus test results from the public hospital labs of the region, from April through August 2009. Their data trace how the new flu arrived and spread during its first season. Such regional records show how a pandemic unfolds on the ground. They also document how lab surveillance worked while the outbreak was still new.
plos-pone-0009314:
Elias César Araujo de Carvalho and co-authors published this data sharing paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Research on disease patterns and clinical care produces valuable data sets. Yet sharing between research groups is poor at best. That hoarding slows science and wastes the effort of the patients and communities who supplied the data.

The authors describe a web application built to share information about such data sets. They also present the policy model that governs who may see what. Describing a data set's contents, without exposing private records, makes collaboration easier. The paper offers a working pattern for opening research data safely.
plos-pone-0011414:
Sebastian Padayatty and colleagues surveyed alternative medicine practitioners in 2010 about giving vitamin C by intravenous drip. High-dose vitamin C through a vein is offered for cancer and other conditions, despite thin evidence and little tracking of harm. Because the practice sits outside standard medicine, no registry recorded how it was used or what went wrong.

The survey asked practitioners how they prepare and dose the vitamin and what adverse effects they had seen in patients. Gathering those reports maps real-world habits and harms that trials had missed. Patients considering the therapy gain a clearer picture of its risks, and regulators gain data where before there were only claims. The study is a model for studying popular alternative treatments honestly: ask the practitioners, record the harms, and publish both.
plos-pone-0011514:
Noelia Valbuena and Sergio Moreno showed in 2010 how fission yeast merges two keep-off signals into one decisive stop. Fission yeast mate and enter meiosis only when food is scarce, and two nutrient-sensing pathways, TOR and PKA, normally block mating in good times. The puzzle was whether the two blocks are independent backups or parts of one mechanism.

Both pathways proved to converge on a single protein, the Ste11 transcription factor, which is the switch that turns on mating genes. Together they hold that switch off more firmly than either could alone. Convergence of this kind is an elegant design: several senses of plenty vote on one switch, so a single faulty sensor cannot trigger mating by mistake. The study explains, in one clean circuit, how cells make a life-or-death decision robust.
plos-pone-0011614:
Benoit Guénard and Robert Dunn reported a hidden ant invasion in eastern North American forests, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Introduced ants threaten native wildlife in many places, yet few foreign species manage to invade cool temperate forests. One ant long treated as a normal forest resident turns out to be something else.

Careful identification showed the ant is an introduced species that arrived long ago and spread widely unnoticed. Because it is now abundant, its effects on forest floors, seeds and other insects may be broad. The case warns that other supposed natives may also be overlooked invaders.
plos-pone-0011714:
Mounia Alaoui-El-Azher and co-authors traced how a gum germ's toxin kills mouth lining cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The toxin, called CDT, comes from the oral germ Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans. It halts the cell cycle and triggers set cell death in several cell types.

With chemical blockers and gene silencing in human gum cells, the team mapped the death route step by step. It runs through the ATM and checkpoint kinase 2 pathway, the cell's DNA damage alarm. Charting each step shows how this mouth poison does its work, and where a drug might cut in.
plos-pone-0011814:
Aaron White and co-authors tied a broad fuel shift to Salmonella group behaviour, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Germs can build complex group patterns set by timed waves of gene use, most often under one master control path. For group builds such as biofilms, the switches that start the process were partly known.

Their work links a sweeping change in fuel use to Salmonella's shift into group life. As the germs band together, their whole energy plan is recast. That fuel switch shows the power plan behind biofilm cities, which are famed for being hard to treat with drugs.
plos-pone-0012014:
Glenda Canderan and colleagues presented in 2010 a recipe for growing a patient's own tumor-fighting T cells in the lab. Expanding killer CD8 T cells that recognize a patient's own non-small cell lung cancer is a goal of tumor immunology, both for research and for therapy. The hard part is doing it efficiently and keeping the cells specific.

Their strategy induces and maintains such T cells in vitro, using the patient's own tumor as the target reference. A dependable recipe matters because cell therapy fails when the product cannot be made the same way twice. Lung cancer is common and often drug-resistant, so a workable autologous cell approach has wide relevance.
plos-pone-0012114:
John Fieberg, Kyle Shertzer, Paul Conn, and co-authors built a model of Minnesota's black bear population for PLOS ONE in 2010. Counting wild bears directly is costly and hard, but records from hunted bears, such as age and sex, are easy to gather. The team combined those harvest records with other data in one model of the whole population.

A single model that uses every data source at once gives a clearer picture than each source read alone. It can estimate how many bears there are and how fast the population is changing. Wildlife managers can then set hunting limits and watch trends with more confidence, using data they already collect each year.
plos-pone-0012214:
Enrico De Franchi, Claire Schalon, Mirko Messa, and co-authors predicted side targets of kinase-blocking drugs by computer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Kinases are switch enzymes that many modern cancer drugs aim to block, but a drug shaped for one often fits others, causing surprise side effects. Their method compares the three-dimensional pockets where drugs bind, measuring how similar one kinase's pocket is to another's.

Similar pockets predict cross-reactions, and the team followed their predictions by testing drugs against an unexpected target, a scaffold protein in nerve endings. Catching off-target binding on a computer, before patients do, is cheaper and safer. The approach can also rescue shelved drugs by revealing new uses.
plos-pone-0012314:
Raúl Guantes, Javier Estrada, and Juan Poyatos analyzed signal detection by genetic circuits in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells run small gene circuits that detect signals. Some read a signal's size. Others read how fast it pulses. All of them must work amid molecular noise. That noise is the random jitter of small numbers of molecules. The authors asked what trade-offs such detection imposes. They also asked how noise limits it.

Their study of a simple circuit shows where two goals pull apart. Those goals are sensitivity and reliability. People who build cell sensors need these limits before they build. The work also explains why natural circuits take the shapes they do. Evolution had to pay the same trade-offs.
plos-pone-0012414:
Noha Youssef, M. Couger and Mostafa Elshahed surveyed microbes at an Oklahoma sulfur spring in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Zodletone Spring hosts a rich mix of bacteria in sharp chemical layers. Deep DNA sequencing now reads far more species than older surveys, letting the team ask how much of the local variety comes from rare species found only in one layer.

Most of the fine-scale variety came from the rare biosphere, species present at very low numbers. Each layer kept its own rare cast. The result warns that shallow sampling misses most diversity and shows why rare microbes, though scarce, may hold unique chemistry worth protecting and studying.
plos-pone-0012514:
Thomas Fischer, Robert Langner, Kersten Diers and colleagues tracked brain waves while people waited for a signal, in a 2010 PLOS ONE EEG study. When a warning cue promises a coming event, the scalp EEG shows a slow negative drift called the contingent negative variation. Its early part reflects anticipation, and faster beta waves ride alongside it.

The team mapped where and when beta activity changed during that early anticipation phase. The pattern locates the brain systems that prepare action before events happen. Anticipation faults appear in conditions from ADHD to Parkinson's disease, so a fine time-space map of normal anticipation is useful reference data.
plos-pone-0012614:
Leimu and Fischer crossed plants from separate populations and watched what happened to their defences. Mixing populations can add fresh genetic variety, which often helps a group survive. It can also backfire, a problem called outbreeding depression, when local traits no longer fit together.

Their 2010 study went beyond plant growth and checked how the crosses handled insect attack and damage. Outbreeding changed both resistance and tolerance, the two ways plants cope with being eaten. The results warn conservation workers that mixing plant populations alters more than size or seed count.
plos-pone-0012714:
Miquel, Peyretaillade, Claret and co-authors published the full genome of a Crohn's disease linked E coli strain. The strain, LF82, clings to and invades gut cells and is found in the ileum of many Crohn's patients. Their 2010 paper reads its complete DNA, letter by letter.

A full genome lets researchers list every tool the strain carries for sticking, invading and surviving inside cells. Comparing it with harmless gut E coli shows which parts are unusual. That inventory guides the search for what makes this strain a Crohn's partner.  The genome is now public for any group to mine.
plos-pone-0012814:
Gessmann, Kourtis, Petratos and co-authors modelled the touch-sensing ion channels found across animals. The DEG/ENaC family of channel proteins serves roles from salt balance to the sense of touch. Their members appear in all animal groups, humans included, yet their detailed shapes long stayed unclear.

Their 2010 modelling study set out the shared structural features of these channels and how those features fit their jobs. A channel that opens under pressure is the basis of touch itself. Models like theirs guide the hunt for drugs acting on pain and blood pressure.
pmc-2563014:
Meyer, Paarmann, D'Souza, and co-authors present the metagenomics RAST server, a public tool for analysing community DNA. Metagenomes are random samples of genomes from microbes living together in soil, water, or the gut. By 2008 the hard part had shifted from producing sequences to making sense of them.

Cheap, high-throughput sequencing flooded labs with data they could not annotate alone. The server automatically sorts sequences by evolutionary origin and by function. A shared public service let small teams study whole microbial communities without building their own computing pipelines.  Results return as tables and pictures that bench scientists can read directly.
pmc-3816614:
Scher, Sczesnak, Longman, and co-authors link growth of the gut germ Prevotella copri to higher risk of arthritis. Rheumatoid arthritis is a common systemic immune disease caused by a mix of genetic and outside factors. Animal models suggest gut bacteria help support the systemic immune response needed for joints to swell.

The team profiled gut microbes in patients and found Prevotella copri expanded in those at risk. That correlation points to the gut as a cause in joint disease. It supports trials of diet or microbe-targeted treatment to prevent arthritis.  The finding shifted attention from joints alone to the gut-joint axis overall.
pmc-4373114:
Nyaga, Arbyn, and Aerts presented Metaprop in 2014, a Stata command for meta-analysis of proportions. Meta-analysis has become an essential way to combine evidence from many similar studies. Proportions, such as the share of patients with a trait, need methods suited to binomial data.

Metaprop produces summary statistics and displays for this common task inside Stata, a package many health researchers already use. Accessible software matters, since a sound method helps no one if few can run it. Pooled proportions inform screening, diagnosis, and disease burden estimates. The command made a specialized analysis a routine option for clinical and population studies.
pmc-4877414:
Greenland, Senn, Rothman, and their co-authors wrote a guide in 2016 to misreadings of statistics. Misinterpretation and abuse of tests, P values, confidence intervals, and power have been criticized for decades, yet remain rampant. No simple reading of these concepts is at once intuitive, correct, and foolproof.

The guide works through the most common wrong readings and shows what each measure actually says. A P value, for instance, is not the probability that a claim is true. Clearer understanding would cut false claims across medicine and science. The paper is widely assigned to researchers who report trial and study results.
pmc-4934014:
Haeussler, Schönig, Eckert, and their co-authors evaluated scoring algorithms for CRISPR guide RNAs in 2016. The success of CRISPR/Cas9 editing depends on choosing the right guide RNA sequence. Various websites help with that choice, each using its own prediction algorithms.

It was unclear how far those predictions agreed with actual editing results. The team tested on-target and off-target scoring methods against measured activity. They then integrated the best findings into CRISPOR, a guide selection tool. Better scoring means fewer wasted edits and fewer unwanted cuts elsewhere in the genome. The evaluation gave CRISPR users an evidence base for picking guides.
pmc-5889714:
Miten Jain, Sergey Koren, Karen Miga, and many colleagues reported a human genome sequenced with nanopore reads in 2018. They used a pocket-sized device that pulls long DNA strands through tiny pores. The reads were far longer than those from older machines.

Long reads let the team assemble stretches that short reads cannot span, including some hard repeat regions. The work also showed direct detection of chemical marks on DNA. Gaps and errors remained, but the proof of principle was strong. The study marked a step toward cheap, portable genome sequencing outside big centers.
pmc-7263814:
Derek Chu and a large international team published a systematic review and meta-analysis in 2020 on three simple barriers against the virus that causes COVID-19. The virus spreads mainly from person to person through close contact. The team gathered studies from health care settings and from everyday settings such as homes and public places.

They weighed the evidence on keeping physical distance, wearing face masks, and protecting the eyes. Their pooled results supported each measure, with larger distances and well fitted masks linked to lower transmission. At a time when no vaccine or cure existed, the review gave governments and hospitals a firm evidence base for rules that many people found burdensome but that slowed the spread.
pmc-7779014:
Jaina Mistry and co-authors described in 2021 the state of Pfam, a database that classifies proteins into families and domains. Sorting a protein into the right family is often the quickest way to guess its job. Since the database was last formally described, its thirty-third release alone added several hundred new families and improved many existing entries.

The article explains how families are built, how entries are refined, and how users can reach the data more easily. It also covers the website and tools that serve the classifications to the research community. Pfam's groupings are woven into countless other databases, so this update documents a piece of shared infrastructure that much of bioinformatics depends on.
pmc-9825514:
The UniProt Consortium reported in 2022 the enhancements behind the 2023 edition of UniProt, the universal protein knowledgebase. UniProt aims to give users a complete, high quality, freely accessible set of protein sequences, each annotated with what is known about its function. It is consulted by researchers in nearly every branch of the life sciences.

The article describes improvements to the data processing pipeline that imports and annotates sequences, and to the website through which users reach them. It also covers how the resource keeps pace with the flood of new sequences while holding its quality bar. These behind the scenes upgrades decide how quickly a newly discovered protein becomes usable knowledge.
plos-pone-0359314:
Leila Sharda and a broad team of co-authors published in 2026 the protocol for a scoping review about dementia care across language and culture. The review will gather what is known about how such care is handled for members of minoritised ethnic groups who have dementia or milder problems with memory and thinking. Language barriers and cultural differences can distort memory tests and delay diagnosis in these communities.

A protocol paper fixes the review's questions and methods in advance, so readers can later judge whether the team followed its own plan. The planned review maps a scattered literature rather than testing one treatment. Its findings should help clinics adapt their assessments so that a person's background does not decide the quality of their dementia care.
plos-pone-0356614:
Sinan Eliaçık and Nouman Ali designed new drug candidates by computer in 2026 for restless legs syndrome, a disorder that drives an urge to move the legs, worst at night. Their target receptors are dopamine D1 and D3, since dopamine signaling is deeply involved in the condition. Starting from rotigotine, a drug already used for it, they aimed to design improved derivatives from scratch, a process called de novo design.

Their pipeline combines a three dimensional convolutional network with a generative model and a sequence model to propose and refine candidate molecules. Computer design of this kind can explore far more chemical possibilities than a laboratory, leaving bench scientists a short list worth making and testing.
plos-pone-0351014:
Putri Amelia and co-authors reviewed the records of child heart patients in Indonesia in 2026, studying three things together: nutrition, the burden of illness, and how much health care the children used. Their retrospective cross-sectional study covers pediatric outpatients living with congenital heart disease, heart defects present from birth. Such children often grow poorly, because a struggling heart burns energy and feeding is hard.

Looking at nutritional status beside clinical burden and clinic use shows where the strain concentrates and which children return most often. plos-pone-0356914:
YiZhong Yang leads a team of five teaching a camera system to sort construction waste on sites, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rubble heaps mix categories that look alike, hide under each other, and bend out of shape, while site computers are weak. Their algorithm trims a detection network for lightness. It adds spatial attention so the model notices where things are. It also redesigns the detection head, aligning what the model sees with what it is asked to find.

On the team's ten category dataset, the system beat its parent network on detection quality and precision while shedding about a fifth of its parameters. The model weighs four megabytes, small enough for cheap site hardware to run in real time. Tests on public datasets backed its ability to generalize beyond its home set. For an industry drowning in debris, automated sorting at the source starts with eyes this cheap.
plos-pone-0357014:
Irène Godéré led a team of eight authors working on microplastics in giant clams, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Giant clams filter seawater for food and swallow plastic particles along the way. Counting those particles inside the clam Tridacna maxima is slow by hand, so the team tested a staining dye called Nile Red with machine learning.

Godéré's combined method aims to spot and count microplastics faster and more reliably. Marine scientists tracking plastic in filter feeders need that speed to survey wide areas. Giant clams are also valued reef animals, so knowing their plastic load serves both pollution science and their protection. The approach could extend to oysters and other filter feeders people eat.
plos-pone-0357214:
Nidal S. Khatib and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on reading cerebral palsy risk from the way young babies kick. Clinicians score infants' spontaneous movements with a trained eye, a scarce skill, so objective measures could widen screening. Twenty-six babies under three months wore motion-capture sensors while kicking; models estimated joint movements and muscle forces, and waveform analysis measured how varied the patterns were.

Variation told the story. Babies whose movements scored as healthier showed richer variation in knee and hip motion and in several muscle forces, while restricted variation tracked with the poor-repertoire pattern that flags risk. Some measures also shifted with age, matching the known path toward more complex movement. A statistical classifier separated normal from poor-repertoire babies with good accuracy using those measures alone. Such measurements, they argue, could support earlier, cheaper risk screening and give physiotherapists concrete targets.
plos-pone-0354114:
Heribert Stich, Angelika Deisling, and Fabian Standl report infection screening results for unaccompanied refugee minors arriving in one Bavarian district of Germany. Long journeys can expose young travelers to infections, and German law requires health checks on arrival. The team reviewed standardized assessments gathered over thirteen years for more than two hundred minors. Tests covered tuberculosis, hepatitis types, scabies, and gut parasites. Journey links were then explored in the subgroup with travel details recorded.

At least one infection was found in about three in five minors screened. Prevalence patterns were broadly similar across journey features in this early analysis. Stich and colleagues argue the high overall rate alone justifies careful screening and fast treatment pathways for this vulnerable group, whatever route they traveled.
plos-pone-0330014:
Mirte Boelens and colleagues refined a questionnaire that measures health broadly, not just the absence of disease. They asked the people who would use and answer it. Their 2026 study convened nine focus groups and an expert interview. Seventy-six participants spanned healthcare, welfare, policy, and research. Citizens, including those on low incomes, took part too. All critiqued the thirty-two-item instrument their team had built earlier.

Items were cut, merged, and added, landing at twenty-eight. Participants pushed for questions about felt experience, like feeling happy or healthy. They pushed against wording that smuggles in judgments. Items on exclusion and belonging sparked genuine disagreement, settled by a preset decision rule. The revised questionnaire is offered for use across health, welfare, and policy settings.
plos-pone-0354714:
Makoto Nishimori and colleagues taught deep learning systems to grade heart muscle inflammation from biopsy slides. Myocarditis can kill quickly, yet the gold-standard biopsy lacks an objective severity score. Their 2026 study used slides from several hundred patients at a national heart centre, with severe cases defined by shock, support machines, or death.

One model scored severity from the density of immune cells counted by a detection system. A second model, reading the most telling slide patches with a transformer, separated severe from milder cases almost perfectly in testing. Its attention maps highlighted both inflammation and muscle injury. Nishimori and colleagues propose the score as a standardised tissue index, pending wider validation.
plos-pone-0355614:
Catiana Engelhardt and colleagues randomly assigned anxious adults to two talking therapies delivered in online groups. Cognitive behaviour therapy is the standard; positive psychotherapy instead builds on strengths and good experiences. Their 2026 trial ran both for ten weeks and measured anxiety, happiness, quality of life, and distress up to three months later.

Patients improved clearly in both groups, with medium to large gains over time. Almost no measure favoured one therapy over the other; a single fear questionnaire was the lone exception. Follow-up scores held the gains. Engelhardt and colleagues read the result as evidence that positive psychotherapy can stand beside the standard approach for anxiety, at least in an online group format.
plos-pone-0355314:
Andrés Velasco-Cárdenas and co-authors sprayed cut-flower plants with natural defence triggers to blunt a major thrips pest. Western flower thrips damage ornamental crops worldwide, and insecticides are losing ground to resistance. Their 2026 study applied two elicitors, methyl jasmonate and a floral scent compound, to Alstroemeria plants and measured feeding damage.

Both triggers cut thrips feeding consistently across doses and time points. The strongest, most repeatable effects came from the higher jasmonate dose and the mid scent dose. Thrips on treated leaves showed shifted detox enzyme activity, and plant chemistry profiles separated clearly by treatment. Velasco-Cárdenas and colleagues present elicitor priming as a residue-light complement to chemical control in floriculture.
plos-pone-0355714:
