Shahida Ferdousee and co-authors stressed four high-yield tomato varieties with salt and with a drought mimic to compare their defences. Salinity and drought are intensifying with climate change and slash tomato harvests. Their 2026 study tracked growth, leaf water, pigments, and protective chemistry across the varieties under both stresses.

No single tolerance pattern emerged; each variety answered differently. One kept growing taller shoots and stockpiled the protective compound proline. Another held its green pigment and leaf water while keeping a damage chemical lowest. Detox enzyme activity shifted with variety, treatment, and their combination. Ferdousee and colleagues say breeders should match variety choice to the stress a region expects most.
plos-pone-0355214:
Farhad Udwadia, Annudesh Liyanage, and Gary Yang study device sales staff in 2026. They ask if a rep in the room changes surgery results. The surgery repairs a swollen belly artery from inside. Reps teach device use and help fix problems. Their presence also raises worries about bias. Records covered ninety planned cases at one busy centre.

A rep was present in most of the cases. No clear gaps appeared in surgery time. Imaging time and extra device use matched as well. Hospital stay and leak rates were alike. Death rates also matched at six months. Routine rep support showed no clear gain here. The authors call for more selective use of reps.
plos-pone-0354814:
Solomon Gedfie led a team of eight authors on this 2026 systematic review of leukemia across Africa. Scattered hospital studies had given conflicting pictures of how common this blood cancer is. The team searched several databases, followed standard review guidelines, and pooled the results with statistical models.

Their combined estimate put leukemia at about five percent in the general population studied, lower in children. Living in a rural area and being older were both linked to higher odds. Gedfie and colleagues argue the pooled picture gives cancer planners a firmer base for deciding where diagnosis and treatment services are most needed.
plos-pone-0354514:
Eline Meireson and five colleagues published this 2026 ultrasound study of the unborn baby's heart. A technique that tracks tiny speckles in ultrasound images can measure how the heart muscle stretches, but doctors worry different users get different numbers. Healthy pregnant volunteers had scans every four weeks, and observers re-measured the same heartbeat blind.

Agreement was steadier for the left side of the heart than the right, and it weakened after about thirty-two weeks of pregnancy. Meireson sees real promise in the method, but says the measurement routine needs tightening before clinics rely on it.
plos-pone-0354914:
Min Sup Lim and four colleagues published this 2026 paper on a faster test for respiratory syncytial virus, a major cause of chest infections in babies and older adults. Standard gene testing needs complex machines, which many clinics lack. Their method copies viral genes at one steady temperature and uses two probes to tell subtype A from subtype B.

The test caught nearly all true cases of both subtypes and never fired on other common respiratory viruses. Lim sees it as a fit for small clinics and field settings, once wider trials confirm the lab results.
plos-pone-0347214:
Iqra Shafique led a team of eight authors on this 2026 lab study attacking drug-resistant typhoid bacteria without antibiotics. Resistant Salmonella typhi strains pump drugs back out of their cells and form protective films. The team tested two plant compounds, schisandrins from a vine, against resistant and sensitive clinical strains.

Schisandrin B disrupted bacterial membranes, blocked the pumps, and stopped most film growth in the lab, slowing the bacteria rather than killing them outright. Shafique argues such non-antibiotic helpers could one day restore the power of failing typhoid drugs, pending much more testing.
plos-pone-0352514:
Stepanian and colleagues, in a 2026 study, sort breast tumors using both their full gene activity and the ancestry of the patients. Breast cancer is the top cancer killer of women worldwide, and precise subtypes guide treatment. Standard subtyping uses a short gene list and can wobble depending on the batch of samples fed in.

The team read RNA from about two hundred seventy tumors and a few healthy samples from varied places. From the same data they extracted enough genetic markers to infer broad ancestry, and they recovered European, African, Asian, South Asian, and mixed American roots. Clustering on complete expression profiles grouped tumors in ways the short list only partly matched. Computer drug tests then pointed to medicines that might work on specific clusters. The authors argue that ancestry-aware, whole-profile subtyping could make breast cancer care fairer and sharper, provided research cohorts grow more diverse.
plos-pone-0331514:
Takakura and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Japan, compare quitting smoking by telemedicine against doing it face to face in clinics. Clinic programs work but demand repeated trips, which many smokers find bothersome. The online program ran four video sessions over eight weeks with drug support, and followed patients for a year.

Thousands of smokers applied online, and a large group was analyzed against clinic patients drawn from a health ministry database. The share who finished treatment was far higher online than in the clinic comparison. Long-term abstinence a year later is the paper's headline measure, set against the burden of travel. The authors frame telemedicine as a way to keep smokers in treatment long enough for the drugs and coaching to work. They note the comparison is retrospective, so the groups were not assigned at random.
plos-pone-0354014:
Lei Ma and four co-authors build a gene-based prediction model for Alzheimer's disease from tiny parcels that cells release into the blood, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. These parcels, called exosomes, carry molecules tied to the disease. Working only with public datasets, the team sifted exosome-related genes for a small set that could flag the disease.

Five genes formed their final model. Computer simulations then linked those genes to several existing drugs and mapped where drug molecules might bind on the resulting proteins. Everything here is computational, with no patient testing yet. Still, a blood-based gene signature of this kind is exactly what early Alzheimer's diagnosis research is hunting for.
plos-pone-0352314:
Mohammad Fathi and seven colleagues train a machine-learning model to grade how badly intensive care patients' kidneys are failing, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Standard staging uses two measures and misses much of the clinical picture. Working with records of more than two thousand patients from a large critical-care database, the team fed dozens of routine variables into a gradient-boosted model and asked which ones carried the signal.

The model sorted patients into the correct severity stage about four times in five, performing best at the extremes — no injury and the most severe injury. Pre-existing kidney disease, sepsis, a liver pigment, and several blood-pressure drugs topped the predictor list. Such models could flag deteriorating kidneys hours before the standard thresholds trip.
plos-pone-0351314:
Le, Nhu, and Thong built a hybrid AI framework to predict drug and protein pairings in a 2026 study. Knowing which proteins a drug touches speeds discovery and reuse of old drugs. Their system reads drug shapes with one network and protein sequences with another, then lets the two views attend to each other.

Tests used two standard benchmark sets under three splits, including hard cases with unseen drugs or unseen proteins. Performance matched leading rival methods across those tests. Gains came from joining shape and sequence views rather than relying on either alone. Better pairing predictions cut the number of lab tests wasted on hopeless combinations.
plos-pone-0353214:
Eleftheria Michalaki and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study of a strikingly cheap device for delivering RNA vaccines without the fatty carriers used today. The gadget, adapted from a lighter and costing under a dollar, uses tiny needles and a small electric pulse to push naked RNA into skin cells. Carrier-free RNA is normally destroyed quickly and enters cells poorly, so it had been written off.

With the device, naked RNA produced strong gene activity and immune responses in animals, matching carrier-based delivery at low doses, without the body-wide inflammation those carriers cause. The team tested several RNA designs and confirmed the approach works in living human skin samples. They pitch it as a low-cost route for routine shots and fast pandemic response.
plos-pone-0351114:
Dana Islam and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One systematic review of immersive virtual reality in stroke rehabilitation. The reviewers gathered randomized trials, thirty-four studies with about twelve hundred survivors in total, testing fully immersive headsets alone or alongside standard therapy for arm movement, balance, walking, and quality of life.

Virtual reality, usually added to conventional rehabilitation, improved upper-limb motor impairment on the standard assessment scale, and small gains appeared in some walking measures. Results for everyday function, balance, and life quality were mixed and hard to pin down. The authors judge the evidence promising but weak, graded low to very low certainty, and call for larger, better-standardized trials before immersive therapy becomes routine.
plos-pone-0339114:
Mohammad Abuawad and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One study of meningioma in Palestine. Meningioma is the most common primary brain tumor. The team worked from records at Al-Makassed Hospital. That hospital is the country's main referral center for brain surgery. They profiled just over two hundred confirmed cases from 2018 to 2023. They logged age, sex, tumor grade, symptoms, and care.

The typical patient was about fifty-one years old. Women were affected at roughly twice the male rate. The authors stress that their rate estimate is a floor, not a true population rate. Most tumors were the lowest grade. Higher grades were more common in men. Local nerve symptoms were the usual first complaint. Nearly all patients were treated with surgery alone. The authors call for registry-style research to firm up the picture.
plos-pone-0350514:
Tu Trang and five colleagues ask the staff who used genome-guided tuberculosis treatment what they really thought of it. Their 2026 study sits inside the SMARTT trial. The trial tested whether whole-genome sequencing, translated into drug recommendations, could improve care for rifampicin-resistant TB. Eleven health workers who managed trial patients joined a focus group. Their experiences were sorted by theme, letting patterns emerge from the conversation itself.

The technology mostly won them over. Sequencing simplified drug susceptibility testing and was seen as good for patients. It did not threaten the workers' professional judgement or autonomy. Trust still cracked in places. Slow result turnaround, advice deviating from guidelines, and disagreement between testing methods all hurt confidence. A few patients' poor outcomes lingered in minds. Stock-outs, patchy internet, and training gaps completed the obstacle list. Genomic medicine's promise, the workers suggest, will live or die on logistics.
plos-pone-0352014:
Claire Peneycad and co-authors studied a plant compound called isoginkgetin, taken from ginkgo leaves, and its odd effect on metal-handling genes. The compound was already known to block cells from making new proteins. The team found it also switches on genes for metallothioneins, small proteins that bind metals, and for a zinc transporter.

The switch runs through a known metal-sensing factor, and the gene messages rose in several cell lines. Yet the matching proteins did not increase, because the compound blocks translation, the step that builds proteins from messages. A reporter test confirmed messages were being read less, not more. The work warns that a rise in gene messages does not always mean more protein, a trap for anyone reading drug effects from RNA alone.
plos-pone-0351414:
Anemia stays common in India even though a national program has pushed iron supplements since 2018. Priyanka Gupta Bansal and colleagues describe the PRAKASH study, a 2026 PLOS One protocol for testing better ways to deliver proven anemia care in real districts.

The plan covers young children, school-age children, teenagers, women of childbearing age, and pregnant women. Its parts include testing and treating until anemia clears, iron and folic acid pills, fortified rice, more iron-rich foods, and public campaigns. Repeated community surveys will measure anemia rates, while interviews probe what helps or blocks the work. The goal is prevalence at or below one fifth.
plos-pone-0349514:
Karolina Pawłowska-Cyprysiak and colleagues asked what shapes whether people with disabilities in Poland take part in training for computer skills. Their 2026 PLOS One survey gathered answers from about four hundred fifty people with different kinds of disabilities.

One factor stood out sharply. When training looked hard to access, through distance, cost, or rooms and materials that ignore disabled users, the chance of taking part fell by more than seventy percent. Other traits mattered far less by comparison. The authors say the lesson is simple: making courses genuinely reachable does more for equal chances than urging people to sign up.
plos-pone-0349414:
Maiya G Block Ngaybe and colleagues interviewed twenty experts and peer leaders in Uganda in March 2024 about HIV prevention choices for groups at highest risk. A long acting injectable prevention drug has been approved but not yet rolled out in Uganda, and a future vaccine may follow. Talks covered current habits and what people would want from injectable options.

Condoms and daily prevention pills were the most mentioned current tools. Barriers named included dosing burden, access, cost, and stigma. Long dosing gaps made injectables attractive, provided supply and privacy hold. Rollout plans that listen to peer leaders first, the authors argue, will decide whether a promising drug is actually used.
plos-pone-0351214:
Hongzhen Yin and colleagues reviewed forty one adults treated for a foreign body stuck in the airway at a Chinese hospital across nearly twelve years. Swallowed or inhaled objects in adults are rare but can kill. Records covered imaging, removal method, breathing support, brain outcome, and survival to twenty eight days.

Flexible scope removal was tried first in nearly all patients and worked in about four fifths. Most patients needed only nasal oxygen, while about one fifth needed stronger support including one case of full life support. Survival at twenty eight days passed ninety percent, and most survivors left with good brain function. A clear pathway keeps rare emergencies calm and successful.
plos-pone-0342114:
Victoria Miller and co-authors reviewed court cases about retinoblastoma, a childhood eye cancer, in work published in 2026. Late diagnosis can cost a child an eye or worse, and the team asked what goes wrong often enough to end in malpractice suits.

A legal database search found thirteen cases covering fourteen children, most of them girls, and all alive at trial. Several suits claimed doctors failed to warn parents about inherited risk, or missed signs. Specialties named ranged from eye doctors to pregnancy care. Though the set is small, it shows families and courts focus on warning, screening, and fast referral.
plos-pone-0350614:
Hriddhi Sarker and co-authors searched for drug targets shared by breast, ovarian, and colorectal cancers in 2026. Cancers differ, yet shared growth pathways may allow one drug to strike several types, a cheaper road than one drug per cancer.

Three gene data sets yielded a common set of changed genes. Network ranking lifted three cell division genes to the top as targets. Pathway and regulator analysis sketched the shared machinery, and docking tests ranked candidate drugs, with one compound binding most strongly. Computer evidence only, but it gives labs a short, shared target list to test in cells.
plos-pone-0350414:
Jean A Hall, Leslie B Hancock, and Elizabeth M Morris fed cats with early kidney disease two special diets to see how the balance of calcium to phosphorus affects blood calcium control. Cats with kidney disease can develop high blood calcium, and diet is a suspected driver. Their 2026 trial rotated nine older cats between a moderate-ratio food and a higher-ratio food, with washout periods between, sampling blood and urine throughout.

Blood calcium stayed within the normal range on both foods, and most calcium-related measures did not differ by diet. The higher-ratio food did lower parathyroid hormone and showed trends toward raising two other markers, all still in normal ranges. The authors conclude that dietary calcium ratio alone is likely not the sole cause of high blood calcium as kidney disease advances, though the shifts they saw deserve further study.
plos-pone-0350014:
Gustavo A Ballen, Klára Hedvika Mühlová, and Jan Hajič jr. applied tools from evolutionary biology to one of music history's puzzles: recovering the earliest forms of Gregorian chant melodies. Early chant notation does not record pitch precisely, so original melodies must be inferred. Legend credits Pope Gregory the First with receiving the chant from a dove, but the tunes evolved over centuries of singing and copying.

The team first converted family trees of chant versions into timed, directed trees, separating elapsed time from rate of change. They then reconstructed likely ancestral melodies at each branching point. Applied to a Christmas Vespers dataset, the results lined up well with what music experts had rebuilt by hand at Solesmes. The authors see the method as a promising way to trace how culture is transmitted through time.
plos-pone-0339014:
Yan Zhang and co-authors studied a chemical arms race in ginger fields, where growing ginger year after year breeds a devastating wilt fungus. Ginger roots release natural compounds, called autotoxins, that slow the crop itself, and the team asked what those same compounds do to the fungus. Their 2026 lab study exposed the pathogen to four ginger autotoxins and tracked its growth, reproduction, and attack tools.

Each compound hit the fungus differently. One strongly curbed growth and spore sprouting yet provoked the fungus to make more wall-chewing enzymes and toxins. Another suppressed nearly everything, including toxin genes. In several cases the fungus answered chemical pressure by raising its own weapons. The authors describe a two-way interaction in which plant defenses and pathogen counterattacks shape the disease.
plos-pone-0350314:
Retraction notice: The PLOS One editors retracted a study claiming that the best stiffness of a three-dimensional gel for keeping cancer stem cells alive depends on the tissue the cancer came from. Editors found multiple figure panels that looked more similar than independent results should, regions within images that appeared discontinuous, and overlap with material published earlier under a restrictive license. The corresponding author attributed the similarities to uniform cell appearance under standardized imaging.

The editors judged the supplied image data incomplete and the explanations insufficient, leaving the reliability of the results in doubt. All authors disagreed with the retraction and stand by their findings, a disagreement the notice records. Because its figures cannot be trusted, the article's claims about matrix stiffness and cancer stem cells should not be relied on.
plos-pone-0348014:
Josna Soyuz and Anish V Cherian led a review of teen suicide research. They focused on a method called psychological autopsy. In it, experts rebuild a young life from records and talks with kin. The aim is to learn what led to the death. The team gathered fifteen such studies. They then drew out the shared themes across them.

Four theme groups came up again and again. The first is the teen's own state: illness of mind, drug use, past self-harm. The second is family strain: sick parents, abuse, neglect. The third is hard life events: school failure, fights, early trauma. The fourth is the world around them: means at hand, media sway, no care near. The team says guard work must act on all four.
plos-pone-0349314:
Abdulrahman Alasmari and colleagues tested an alcohol extract of the plant Otostegia fruticosa against aggressive breast cancer cells in the laboratory. Their 2026 study used MDA-MB-231 cells, a standard model of triple-negative breast cancer, a form that is hard to treat. They measured whether the extract could kill the cells or slow their spread.

The extract did kill the cancer cells, largely by raising reactive oxygen species, unstable molecules that damage cell power plants and trigger cell death. Treated cells also moved and invaded less than untreated ones. The work is early and limited to cells in dishes, but it marks the plant as a candidate for further study.
plos-pone-0348814:
Alejandro Morales-Huitrón and colleagues mapped friendship and hostility among roughly four thousand three hundred students in nine schools in Yucatán, Mexico. From these maps they built two smaller networks: one around students who name many enemies, and one around students who are named as enemies by many others. They then compared the shape of the two networks and how groups formed inside them.

The two networks turned out to overlap heavily, sharing about three fifths of their members, so the same students often appear on both sides of conflict. Girls' networks were generally denser than boys'. The authors connect their measures to roles seen in bullying, and they pin down when these attack and defense networks are defined sharply enough to mean something.
plos-pone-0349114:
Limin Yu, Zhe Chen, and Zeyu Qin tackle a grading problem: hands-on courses taught through real projects need fair marks, yet judges often disagree and their scores carry doubt. Their framework grades students in stages, moving from a pass check to a score and then a final grade. It uses a maths tool built to hold both a judgement and how reliable that judgement is.

Marks came from classmates, teachers, and industry experts for a class of twenty-four students. The weight of each criterion was set by how much it varied and overlapped with others. Repeated checks suggested the method stays stable under changed assumptions. The authors say it can make project course grading clearer and more open, while noting that wider testing in other courses is still needed.
plos-pone-0349614:
Chao Zhang and colleagues trained an artificial intelligence system to spot stomach cancer that has quietly spread to the abdominal lining, a finding that changes whether surgery makes sense. Standard scans often miss this spread in advanced cancers. The team tested several image-reading networks on pre-surgery CT scans and then added attention modules that teach the network where to look hardest.

The best design, a deep network sharpened by a squeeze-and-excitation module, distinguished spread from no spread with excellent accuracy, and its risk estimates matched real outcomes closely. Decision analysis suggested using it would help more patients than it harmed. The authors recommend that patients the system flags as high risk receive a keyhole inspection before any major operation, sparing others futile surgery.
plos-pone-0348714:
Xiaomin Liang and colleagues examined how the tiniest pores inside coal govern how easily trapped methane escapes, a question that matters for both gas production and mine safety. Coals of three ranks, from soft lignite to hard anthracite, were measured for pore size, surface, and connections, then watched as they released methane. The team sorted micropores by how they sit: attached to channels, clustered in networks, or isolated.

Micropores supplied nearly all the surface area, and their arrangement changed with rank. Lignite's attached pores let methane slip straight into flow paths, giving the fastest release. Coking coal's tangled clusters slowed diffusion, and anthracite's isolated pores trapped gas worst of all. The authors link pore layout directly to release behaviour, offering guidance for choosing where and how to drain gas before mining.
plos-pone-0349014:
Jasmijn E Klapwijk and a large team gave fifty-one medical students a set of imaginary cases from prenatal genome testing, where results during pregnancy often come back uncertain. Students judged how uncertain each result felt, decided whether they would pass it to the expectant parents, and rated their confidence in that choice. Their personal tolerance for uncertainty was also measured.

Students passed on fewer of the highly uncertain results and felt shakier about those decisions, confirming a widely held hunch with real data. Surprisingly, students who personally disliked uncertainty behaved no differently from tolerant peers, and anxiety about parents considering ending a pregnancy did not sway reporting either. The authors say counselling training should prepare clinicians for the discomfort of uncertain results, since instinct alone trims what parents get told.
plos-pone-0348514:
Huifu Li and colleagues asked whether building a digital economy cleans the air in China's in-between places, the cities sitting on provincial borders, which often become pollution havens nobody governs well. Panel data from one hundred and eighty-eight border cities over a decade were used to test the link, and to check whether cleaner air spills across borders into neighbouring regions.

Digital development did improve local air quality, with the strongest gains in poorer, less connected border areas. Benefits also leaked helpfully into adjacent regions rather than merely pushing pollution onto them, the opposite of the haven fear. Two channels did the work: digital tools broke down segmented local markets that shelter dirty industries, and they sharpened environmental monitoring and enforcement. The authors offer the findings to developing countries wrestling with the same border problem.
plos-pone-0348614:
Younes Beniaich and co-workers record sleep and movement in newborn lambs across their first three days and again weeks later. As lambs begin chewing the cud, their digestion matures and their days may reorganize. Their 2026 study fits eight lambs with gentle brain and body recorders for three-day stretches at birth and after cud chewing begins.

Newborns were most active around dawn and dusk and slept in many short bouts, more at night. Weeks later, daytime activity rose and total sleep fell by hours, squeezed by time spent chewing the cud. Wake time itself barely changed. Chewing the cud seems to compete directly with sleep as young ruminants grow, a trade-off farmers and vets rarely count.
plos-pone-0348414:
Suhyun Hwangbo, Yoojin Choi, and Jae Yong Ryu built prediction models for triple-negative breast cancer, the subtype with the fewest treatment options and the grimmest outlook. Pooling several gene-expression datasets, they searched for a compact set of genes whose activity forecasts survival, aiming to beat the accuracy ceiling that earlier models had hit.

Their nine-gene signature pushed predictive performance above the level previous studies had managed, and it held up when applied to five independent datasets. Most of the nine genes are individually tied to survival in this cancer. The authors propose the panel as a prognostic marker set to guide follow-up and trial design, pending clinical validation.
plos-pone-0348214:
Qike Fu and colleagues test a malaria drug cousin against diabetic liver damage in mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The drug is artemether, kin to the malaria cure artemisinin. Early work hinted it eases high blood sugar. The liver suffers quietly in type 1 diabetes. No targeted treatment exists for that injury.

In diabetic mice, the drug eased liver harm. It also fixed two deeper faults. The power plants inside liver cells kept a healthier shape. The cells' core fuel chemistry ran more smoothly too. These power plants are the mitochondria. The findings rest on animals only. Still, they point to guarding cell power as a path worth testing.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
The first new state of the new century applied days after its birth. On 23 May 2002, the Council adopted Resolution 1414 without dissent. East Timor had won freedom three days before. A UN-run transition had led it out of Indonesian rule. A quarter century of struggle lay behind the vote.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit East Timor. The Assembly seated it that September. Few entries carried such weight of meaning. The UN had run the land's affairs during the change-over years. It then handed over a working state. Membership closed the long arc from occupation to self-rule.

Housekeeping rarely makes history, but this text fixes the Council's own calendar. In December 1946 the General Assembly set member terms to run from January to December. The Council's rotating presidency still turned monthly on older dates. Resolution 14, dated 16 December 1946, lined the two systems up.

Rule 18, which governs the presidency's rotation, was suspended briefly. The American representative would stay as Council president. His extra stretch ran from 17 December to 31 December 1946. The vote was nine to none. The Soviet Union and, politely, the United States abstained. From then on, presidencies and terms would start together each January.

Resolution 314, adopted on 28 February 1972 by thirteen votes to none with two abstentions, refuses to let Rhodesia sanctions fade. Some states had ignored the mandatory measures imposed in 1968 against the illegal white minority regime, helping it survive. The Council studied the sanctions committee's fourth report and an interim report from December 1971.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council reaffirmed that the sanctions would stay fully in force until their aims were completely achieved. It urged every state to apply all the sanctions resolutions in full, as the Charter requires. It also deplored the attitude of governments that had kept giving the illegal regime moral, political, and economic support.

Resolution 214, adopted on 27 September 1965, shows a ceasefire failing in real time. India and Pakistan had accepted the Council's demand for a ceasefire in the Kashmir war, yet the Secretary-General's reports showed it was not holding. The Council expressed grave concern at the breakdown of a pledge both governments had made unconditionally.

It demanded that the parties urgently honor their commitment to observe the ceasefire. It further called on them to withdraw all armed personnel promptly, as the necessary step toward carrying out resolution 211, the Council's fuller ceasefire and withdrawal order from a week earlier. The war ended within days under combined diplomatic and military pressure, and a settlement conference followed at Tashkent.

The Iran-Iraq war, then nearly two years old, is taken up again in Resolution 514, adopted unanimously on 12 July 1982. The Council said it was deeply concerned at the conflict's prolongation, the heavy loss of life, and the material damage, all endangering peace and security. Mediation by the Secretary-General, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the Islamic Conference had not stopped the fighting.

The Council called for a ceasefire, with all fighting stopped at once. It further called for forces to pull back behind the borders the world recognizes. It decided to send a team of UN observers to verify, confirm, and supervise both steps, and asked the Secretary-General to report on the arrangements needed.

Resolution 114, adopted unanimously on 4 June 1956, follows up the Secretary-General's peace mission to the Middle East. Dag Hammarskjöld had traveled for the Council that spring and won assurances from all parties to the armistice agreements to observe the ceasefire unconditionally. Some specific safety measures he proposed were being adopted, but full compliance with the agreements was still missing.

The Council praised both the Secretary-General's mission and the ground gained so far. It declared that the parties should quickly carry out the measures already agreed with him. It also told them to cooperate with him and with the truce supervision chief of staff to put more of the agreed steps into effect.

Resolution 414, adopted without a vote in September 1977, warns against faits accomplis around Famagusta in Cyprus. Cyprus's ambassador had written in August about developments in the new Famagusta area, the resort district of Varosha, emptied in 1974 and held behind fences. Statements to the Council indicated that no settlement of the area was in fact under way, and the parties and the Secretary-General addressed the reports.

The Council expressed concern at the situation and called on everyone to avoid unilateral actions anywhere in Cyprus that might damage the chances of a just and peaceful solution. It voiced concern at the lack of progress in the intercommunal talks and urged the two communities' representatives to resume negotiations under the Secretary-General as soon as possible.

Yemen's political crisis is addressed in Resolution 2014, adopted on 21 October 2011. Months of protests had met force from the authorities, and hundreds of people, mostly civilians, had died. The Gulf Cooperation Council had put forward a plan for a transfer of power. Food and fuel prices were soaring, hunger was spreading, and Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula was gaining ground in parts of the country.

The Council strongly condemns the rights abuses by Yemen's authorities and by other actors and says those to blame must be held to account. It demands that all sides give up violence as a path to political goals. It backs signing and carrying out the Gulf plan at once, for a Yemeni-led shift to a new government and early presidential elections. It demands open access for aid and asks the Secretary-General to report within 30 days and every 60 days after that.

Somalia's collapse fills Resolution 814, adopted in March 1993. Famine and drought, compounded by civil war, had destroyed the country's means of production. The US-led Unified Task Force, UNITAF, had opened a secure space for relief work under Resolution 794. A transition to an expanded UN Operation in Somalia, UNOSOM II, was now needed, while violence continued and disarmament of the factions remained essential.

The Council approves the Secretary-General's report of 3 March 1993, which set out that transition. It thanks him for convening the Conference on National Reconciliation in Addis Ababa, following the January meeting where Somali parties signed three agreements. It stresses broad representation at such talks, including community leaders, women, professionals, and elders. Throughout, the text insists Somalis themselves bear the final responsibility for reconciliation and rebuilding, and that relief and the revival of institutions and the economy must go together.

UNPROFOR reinforcements are authorized by Resolution 914, adopted on 27 April 1994. The UN Protection Force was stretched across Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina as the wars there went on. The Secretary-General had sent a series of reports and a letter in March 1994 recommending more personnel. The Council said it was determined to strengthen the force so it could fulfil its mandate, and to protect its security and freedom of movement.

Acting under Chapter VII for UNPROFOR in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Council welcomes the Secretary-General's reports. It authorizes an increase of up to 6,550 additional troops, 150 military observers, and 275 civilian police monitors. This comes on top of the reinforcement already approved in Resolution 908 (1994) a month earlier. The Council decides to remain actively seized of the matter.

Somalia's political process is pushed forward in Resolution 1814, adopted on 15 May 2008. Talks between Somali parties had just opened in Djibouti. The Secretary-General proposed an integrated UN strategy. He also proposed moving the UN Political Office for Somalia, UNPOS, from Nairobi into Somalia. Contingency planning was under way for a UN peacekeeping operation to succeed AMISOM. The humanitarian situation kept worsening.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backs the strategy and the UNPOS relocation, with security arrangements to be set. It asks UNPOS to help the Transitional Federal Institutions write a constitution and hold a referendum and elections in 2009. It asks the Sanctions Committee to recommend, within 60 days, targeted measures against those blocking peace, threatening the institutions or AMISOM, or breaking the arms embargo. It calls for full AMISOM deployment, protection for World Food Programme shipping, and safe, unhindered aid delivery.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution 48/114 was adopted by the General Assembly on 20 December 1993. It called for emergency aid to refugees and displaced persons in Azerbaijan. The Assembly voiced grave concern as fighting drove large numbers of civilians from their homes. It noted that the count of refugees and displaced persons in the country had lately passed one million.

The text welcomed the aid work of the United Nations interim office in Azerbaijan. It also welcomed the work of the refugee agency there. It thanked states and aid groups already helping. It urgently appealed for more money, medical help, food, and shelter, above all for winter. It asked the Secretary-General to keep watching the crisis and report back.

General Assembly Resolution 14, from the first session in 1946, set the budget and finance ground rules for the new United Nations. The Assembly said United Nations money matters had to be run in a thrifty, open way. Member states had to be able to trust them. The Assembly adopted the provisional financial regulations reproduced in annex I.

The text created an Advisory Committee on Administrative and Budgetary Questions. It had nine members, and it was to review the budget. The text also created a standing Committee on Contributions of ten. That committee was to work out how costs would be shared. The text covered travel costs for delegates. It voted 21,500,000 dollars for the Assembly, the Councils, the Secretariat, the Court, and unforeseen costs.

General Assembly Resolution 3314 (XXIX), adopted on 14 December 1974 without a vote, approved the Definition of Aggression drafted by its Special Committee. The Assembly called on all states to shun aggression and other unlawful force. It pointed the Security Council to the definition as a guide. The Council was to use it when judging whether an act of aggression has taken place.

The annexed definition calls aggression the use of armed force by one state against another's sovereignty, land, or freedom, against the Charter. It lists acts that count, among them invasion, bombing, blockade, and sending armed bands. It states that no cause of any kind can excuse aggression. It calls a war of aggression a crime against world peace.

Resolution 69/14 of the General Assembly, from 2014, takes note of cooperation between the United Nations and the Organization for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. The Assembly welcomes the joint mission that had just wiped out Syria's chemical weapons program, closing on 30 September 2014. It welcomes the organization's support for the United Nations investigation into alleged chemical weapons use there. It also notes the review conference of 2013 for the chemical weapons convention. It notes plans to mark the centenary of the first large-scale chemical attack in 2015.

Resolution ES-10/14 of the General Assembly was adopted at the tenth emergency special session in October 2003. It addresses illegal Israeli actions in occupied East Jerusalem and the rest of the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Its central concern is the wall then being built by Israel inside the territory, including in and around East Jerusalem.

The Assembly demands that Israel stop and reverse construction of the wall. The wall departs from the Armistice Line of 1949. In its view, it contradicts international law. It could make a two-state solution physically impossible. It condemns suicide bombings, including a recent attack in Haifa, and a bomb attack in Gaza that killed three American security officers. It deplores extra-judicial killings. It calls on both parties to carry out their obligations under the Road Map. It asks the Secretary-General to report on compliance within one month.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Children in wartime stand at the centre of this broad text from 11 August 2000. It builds on a 1999 resolution and on a new world treaty that bars the use of child soldiers. Reports on war-affected children, and meetings held in Ghana and Canada, shaped what the Council wrote.

Deliberate attacks on children and the use of children as soldiers are condemned in strong terms. States are urged to sign and ratify the new treaty, and armed groups are pressed to protect children, free those they abducted, and let aid reach them. Peace deals, the Council adds, should include plans to disarm child soldiers and return them to normal life.

Côte d'Ivoire's special political mission, MINUCI, is extended on 13 November 2003, until 4 February 2004. The mission supports the Linas-Marcoussis peace agreement and the Government of National Reconciliation. The Secretary-General is asked to report by 10 January 2004 on the mission's work and on whether the United Nations presence in the country should be reinforced.

Lebanon's force, UNIFIL, is extended until 31 January 2006 on 29 July 2005. The Secretary-General's July report is endorsed. Grave concern is voiced at the persistence of tensions and recent incidents across the Blue Line, the withdrawal line confirmed after Israel's 2000 pullout.

All acts of violence, including the recent cross-line incidents, are condemned. Lebanon's government is called on to extend its authority fully over the south and do more to secure the area. Both parties are told to give UNIFIL complete freedom of movement and to respect the Blue Line in its entirety. The renewal kept the force's interim mandate in place for another six months.

A judge of the International Court of Justice resigned in 2010, and Resolution 1914 deals with filling his seat. The Court is the main court of the United Nations. Judge Shi Jiuyong had resigned, with the resignation due to take effect on 28 May 2010. The Council adopted the resolution on 18 March 2010.

Under the Court's own rules, the Security Council fixes the date of the election for a new judge. The Council set that election for 29 June 2010. It would be held at a meeting of the Security Council and, on the same day, at a meeting of the General Assembly. Both bodies had to vote to fill the vacancy for the rest of the judge's term.
un-sc-res-14: The Council tidied its own house in December 1946. The General Assembly had set the terms of elected Council members to run by calendar year. The monthly rotation of the Council presidency did not match those dates. On 16 December 1946 the Council suspended its rule 18 for a short period. That let the United States representative stay as president from 17 to 31 December. The presidency would then rotate in step with the calendar.
un-sc-res-314:
Sanctions against Southern Rhodesia were reaffirmed at full strength by the Security Council on 28 February 1972. Some states had failed to apply resolution 253 (1968), against their duty under Article 25 of the Charter. The sanctions committee had sent its fourth report and an interim report of December 1971. The Council acted under its earlier Chapter VII decisions on Rhodesia.

The Council confirmed that sanctions would stay fully in force until the goals of resolution 253 (1968) were completely met. It urged all states to apply every sanctions resolution and deplored those that kept giving the illegal regime moral, political, and economic help. Any law meant to allow imports from Rhodesia, including chrome ore, was declared a breach of states' duties. The committee was told to meet urgently on ways to tighten enforcement of the embargo.
un-sc-res-214: India and Pakistan had agreed to a cease-fire in Kashmir, but it was not holding when the Security Council acted on 27 September 1965. The Council voiced grave concern that the truce accepted by both governments was breaking down. Its demands in resolutions 209, 210, and 211 (1965) had been unanimous. The Council demanded that both parties honor their promise to observe the cease-fire without delay. It further called on them to withdraw all armed personnel promptly, as full application of resolution 211 required.
un-sc-res-514:
The Iran-Iraq war drew a direct cease-fire order from the Security Council on 12 July 1982. The conflict was dragging on with heavy loss of life and great material damage. Mediation had been tried by the Secretary-General, the Non-Aligned Movement, and the Islamic Conference. Resolution 479 (1980) had called for restraint at the war's start, to no lasting effect.

The Council called for a cease-fire and an immediate end to all military operations. It called further for forces to withdraw to internationally recognized boundaries. A team of United Nations observers would be sent to verify, confirm, and supervise the halt and the pullback. The Secretary-General had to report on the arrangements needed. All other states were told to avoid any act that could keep the war going. Mediation through the Secretary-General was to continue toward a full, just settlement of every open issue between the two countries.
un-sc-res-114:
Cease-fire promises in Palestine were weighed by the Security Council on 4 June 1956. The Secretary-General had made a mission on the Council's behalf and reported on it. All parties to the General Armistice Agreements had assured him they would observe the cease-fire without conditions. Some of the practical measures of resolution 113 (1956) were moving forward, but full compliance was not yet in place.

The Council praised the progress made. It declared that the agreed measures should be carried out quickly. The parties had to work with the Secretary-General and the truce chief of staff on the remaining proposals. United Nations observers needed full freedom of movement along the armistice lines, in the demilitarized zones, and in the defensive areas. The Council backed the view that restoring full compliance was a stage on the road to peace. The truce chief would keep watching the cease-fire and reporting.
un-sc-res-414:
Fresh fears over Famagusta's empty quarter reached the Council in 1977. Cyprus's letter of 26 August 1977 raised recent moves in the new Famagusta area. Statements to the Council said no settlement was under way there. The intercommunal talks had made little progress. The Council judged quick movement on the whole Cyprus problem urgent.

The Council voiced concern at the state of affairs caused by the new developments. It called on the parties to shun every unilateral act anywhere in Cyprus that could harm the chances of a just and peaceful settlement. Resolution 365 (1974) and resolution 367 (1975) were restated, with a fresh call to apply them urgently and in full. Concern was voiced at the talks' lack of progress. The two communities' representatives were called to resume talks under the Secretary-General at the earliest date, with comprehensive and concrete proposals on the table.
un-sc-res-2014:
Yemen's crisis drew the Council's first resolution on 21 October 2011. Months of protest had met force, and hundreds lay dead, most of them civilians, women and children among them. The Gulf Cooperation Council's initiative offered a transfer of power. The Secretary-General's good offices and his special adviser's visits were under way. The Human Rights Council had called for a full inquiry into abuses.

The Council voiced profound regret at the hundreds of deaths. It strongly condemned the Yemeni authorities' continued rights violations, above all the excessive force used against peaceful protesters. Every side had to reject violence as a path to political goals at once. The Council restated that signing and applying a settlement on the Gulf initiative's basis was the best way out. The authorities had to honor humanitarian and human rights law instantly. Opposition groups were urged to commit fully to the settlement process.
un-sc-res-814:
Somalia was taken up by the Security Council in Resolution 814, adopted on 26 March 1993. A United States-led task force had opened the way for food aid during the famine. The Council now prepared a full United Nations operation to take its place. Fifteen Somali movements had just agreed to a cease-fire and talks in Addis Ababa.

Acting under Chapter VII, the text creates the expanded operation, UNOSOM II, through 31 October 1993. The new force may use enforcement action to keep aid routes safe across the whole country. It must disarm factions, guard ports and airports, and clear mines. It should also help refugees go home and help Somalis rebuild a police force and a state.
un-sc-res-914:
Bosnia and Croatia are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 914, adopted on 27 April 1994. The United Nations Protection Force, UNPROFOR, was stretched thin on the ground. New cease-fire tasks in central Bosnia and around Sarajevo needed far more staff. The Secretary-General had sent the Council a series of reports that March.

The text approves up to 6,550 extra troops for UNPROFOR. It also allows 150 more military observers and 275 civilian police monitors. The additions come on top of a boost already granted weeks earlier. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council stresses that the force must stay safe and free to move in both republics.
un-sc-res-1814:
Somalia was the matter before the Council in Resolution 1814, adopted on 15 May 2008. Talks between Somali parties had just opened in Djibouti on 12 May. The relief situation was getting worse, and aid work stayed hard and risky. The United Nations political office for Somalia still sat in Nairobi, outside the country.

The Council backs one joined-up United Nations strategy for peace and stability in Somalia. It approves moving the political office and country team into Somalia, with safety plans set first. The sanctions committee has sixty days to propose targeted measures against spoilers and embargo breakers. Planning continues for a peacekeeping force that could one day take over from the African Union mission.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Sudan is the subject of Security Council resolution 1714, adopted in October 2006. The Council had a large peacekeeping mission in southern Sudan, UNMIS, sent to guard the peace deal that ended the long north-south civil war. Darfur, in the west, was burning at the same time, which sharpened every debate on Sudan.

The resolution extends the mandate of UNMIS and restates support for the peace deal between Khartoum and the south. It also voices concern over Darfur and the safety of aid workers. The text shows the Council trying to hold one peace together while another crisis grew.
europmc-pmc10028514:
Eysenbach reflects on the role of ChatGPT and similar AI tools in medical education in a 2023 paper. ChatGPT launched in late 2022 and reached a huge user base within two months. Teachers faced a tool that could write fluent medical text on demand, for good and for ill.

The paper takes the form of a conversation with ChatGPT itself about its classroom role. It weighs uses in learning and writing against risks to honesty and skill. It ends with a call for papers on the theme. The piece captures an early moment of change in medical training.
europmc-pmc10369014:
Chen and colleagues modelled the world cost of a chronic lung disease from 2020 to 2050. The disease is COPD, in which air flow out of the lungs slowly worsens. It is the third top cause of death in the world. The team built an economic model for 204 nations and areas.

Their model counts lost work from illness and death, plus care costs that drain savings. Chen puts the total loss at 4.326 trillion dollars over the 30 years. That is like a yearly tax of 0.111% on world output. China bears the largest share, at 1.363 trillion, with the USA next at 1.037 trillion. The team urges states to invest now to curb the disease.
europmc-pmc10583314:
Zhang and co-authors tested a blood index in 2023 as a death risk mark for heart patients with diabetes. The index, called TyG, joins blood fats and blood sugar in one number. The team drew 1,072 US adults with heart disease and diabetes or pre-diabetes from a national survey. Death records were tracked through 2019.

Over 7,541 person-years, 461 people died, 154 of them from heart causes. Zhang found a U-shaped link between the index and death risk. Risk bottomed near a TyG of 9.05 for all deaths and 8.84 for heart deaths. Below those points, higher values meant lower risk. Above them, higher values meant higher risk. The mark may help flag patients who need closer care.
europmc-pmc10719114:
Yao led a large team in 2023 to chart cell types across the whole mouse brain with place and gene data. The team read genes in about 7 million single cells. Near 4.3 million cells also got a place on a spatial map. The two views merged into one atlas of the adult brain.

The atlas stacks 5,322 clusters into 1,201 supertypes, then 338 subclasses, and at last 34 classes. Yao found that gene identity matched place closely for most types. The top half of the brain held fewer but more distinct nerve cell types. The lower half held more types, each closer kin to the next. A code of gene switches defined types across all regions.
europmc-pmc10730214:
Gavzy and co-authors reviewed Bifidobacterium in 2023, a gut bacterium genus with calming effects on the immune system. These friendly microbes live in the guts of many mammals. When they thin out or vanish, immune balance can slip toward self-attack. Their surface parts and waste products carry much of their signal.

The cells boost Treg cells, the immune arm that damps attack, Gavzy reports. They also firm the gut wall seal and tune other immune cells nearby. Two swelling programs in the gut, Th2 and Th17, get dialled down. The review sorts the paths by which molecule does the work. It ties those paths to the wider gut microbe mix as well.
europmc-pmc1215514:
Agarwal, Gupta, and Sharma reviewed oxidative stress in female fertility in 2005. Reactive oxygen species are active molecules cells make each day. Antioxidants keep them in balance in a healthy body. When that balance tips, stress harms tissues.

These molecules play two roles in the female tract. At low levels they signal normal steps like egg release. At high levels they damage eggs, embryos, and DNA. Stress also links to early labor and fertility decline with age. Agarwal shows antioxidants may guard eggs during ovulation. It appeared in Reproductive Biology and Endocrinology.
europmc-pmc1241714:
Schecter and co-authors reported flame retardant levels in United States breast milk in 2003. No prior study had measured PBDEs in milk from single American mothers. PBDEs come from foam, resin, and plastic products in homes. Use was allowed in the United States but banned in parts of Europe.

European milk levels looked low but rising, possibly peaking in late-1990s Sweden. American data were nearly absent before this work. The team extended its earlier milk studies on dioxins and PCBs. Schecter fills a national gap on infant exposure to persistent chemicals.
europmc-pmc1312014:
Rhodius and co-authors compared a bacterial stress response across related genomes in 2006. Bacteria meet stress by switching on alternative sigma factors. These factors steer gene-copying machinery to stress gene sets. Predicting their target sites is hard because patterns vary.

A validated model predicted 89 sigma E controlled units in E. coli. Predictions extended to eight related genomes. The shared core ensures building blocks of the outer membrane. It covers lipopolysaccharide and porin proteins, the membrane essentials. The variable portion points to disease-related jobs instead. Rhodius separates universal stress duties from species-specific ones.
europmc-pmc1481614:
How staff feel about safety in a ward may shape patient harm. Sexton and co-authors tested a survey for those attitudes in 2006, the Safety Attitudes Questionnaire. They gave it to 10,843 health workers in 203 clinical areas across three countries.

Six attitude themes fit the answers well: teamwork climate, job satisfaction, stress recognition, working conditions, safety climate, and views of management. The scales scored high on reliability, at 0.9. Attitudes varied widely within and between hospitals. Sexton offers the survey as a benchmark tool. Hospitals can compare scores, target weak spots, and check whether fixes shift attitudes over time.
europmc-pmc1665414:
Poor diet may decide whether air pollution harms a pregnancy. Kannan and co-authors built a framework for that question in 2006. Particles in air are linked to low birth weight, stunted growth in the womb, and early delivery.

They outline five plausible pathways, running through oxidative stress, inflammation, clotting, vessel function, and blood flow control. Nutrition touches each of those pathways. So the same pollution dose may harm a poorly nourished mother more. Kannan proposes studies that measure diet and pollution together, rather than treating either in isolation.  The framework also gives clear strategies for testing the model in future studies.
europmc-pmc1854914: Gamma oscillations in human primary somatosensory cortex reflect pain perception. — a 2005 science paper on pain brain waves. It finds gamma waves track pain. The paper is the pain-wave study: the findings on pain perception, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1868914: Molecular biogeography of Europe: Pleistocene cycles and postglacial trends. — a 2005 science paper on Europe's gene map. It charts the ice-age cycles for labs. The paper is the gene-map study: the notes on Europe's genes, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc1906714: The temporal dynamics model of emotional memory processing: a synthesis on the neurobiological basis of stress-induced amnesia, flashbulb and traumatic memories — a 2005 science paper on emotional memory models. It synthesizes the memory research. The paper is the memory-model study: the findings on emotional ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc1950214: Beta-catenin signaling plays a disparate role in different phases of fracture repair: implications for therapy to improve bone healing. — a 2005 science paper on beta-catenin in bone repair. It finds the disparate roles. The paper is the bone-repair study: the findings on fracture ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2265414: IFN-lambda (IFN-lambda) is expressed in a tissue-dependent fashion and primarily acts on epithelial cells in vivo. — a 2005 science paper on IFN-lambda tissue action. It finds the tissue-dependent action. The paper is the IFN-lambda study: the findings on epithelial ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2267814: Episodic sexual transmission of HIV revealed by molecular phylodynamics. — a 2005 science paper on on-off HIV spread. It charts the on-off spread for labs. The paper is the spread-chart study: the notes on HIV, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2329914: The itinerary of autophagosomes: from peripheral formation to kiss-and-run fusion with lysosome — a 2008 science paper on cell-cleanup trips. It tracks the cleanup trips for labs. The paper is the trip study: the notes on cell ills, filed here in full session today.
europmc-pmc2394514: Expression analysis of G Protein-Coupled Receptors in mouse macrophages. — a 2008 science paper on GPCRs in mouse macrophages. It analyzes the receptor expression. The paper is the expression study: the findings on mouse ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2563014: The metagenomics RAST server - a public resource for the automatic phylogenetic and functional — a 2008 science paper on the RAST server. It guides the metagenomics server. The paper is the RAST guide: the findings on the tool, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2570914: Wild ducks as long-distance vectors of highly pathogenic avian influenza virus (H5N1). — a 2008 science paper on ducks spreading flu. It maps the wild-duck vectors. The paper is the vector study: the findings on influenza, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2588614: Left inferior frontal gyrus is critical for response inhibition. — a 2008 science paper on the left frontal gyrus. It proves the gyrus is critical. The paper is the gyrus study: the findings on brain ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2627714: Food-related illness and death in the United States. — a 2008 science paper on US food illness. It counts the food illness and death. The paper is the count study: the findings on food ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2667514: CNV-seq, a new method to detect copy number variation using high-throughput sequencing. — a 2008 science paper on the CNV-seq method. It detects the copy-number variation. The paper is the CNV-seq guide: the findings on copy ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2672614: Global functional atlas of Escherichia coli encompassing previously uncharacterized proteins. — a 2008 science paper on the E. coli atlas. It maps the global atlas. The paper is the atlas study: the findings on E. coli, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2686714: Infrastructure for the life sciences: design and implementation of the UniProt website. — a 2008 science paper on the UniProt website. It designs the life-science infrastructure. The paper is the UniProt guide: the findings on the website, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2701414: Comprehensive comparative-genomic analysis of type 2 toxin-antitoxin systems and related mobile — a 2008 science paper on toxin-antitoxin systems. It compares the genomic systems. The paper is the system study: the findings on toxin ills, filed here in session today.
europmc-pmc2718614: Aging and environmental exposures alter tissue-specific DNA methylation dependent upon CpG isla — a 2008 science paper on aging and DNA methylation. It alters the tissue-specific methylation. The paper is the methylation study: the findings on aging ills, filed here in session.
europmc-pmc2726614: Penetration of the stigma and style elicits a novel transcriptome in pollen tubes, pointing to — a 2008 science paper on pollen-tube transcriptomes. It elicits the novel transcriptome. The paper is the transcriptome study: the findings on pollen ills, filed here in session.
chretien-erec-et-enide-comfort-1914:
W. W. Comfort translated Chretien de Troyes's Erec et Enide into English in 1914. Chretien composed the romance around 1170 in northern France. It is the first Arthurian romance, the work that founded a tradition.

Knight Erec wins the lady Enide and marries her in joy. Then whispers that marriage has softened him drive the couple back to adventure. Enide rides with him, forbidden to speak, yet warns him of dangers. Their trials test love, obedience, and knightly honor together. Comfort's translation opened Chretien to English readers in modern prose. European letters learned the chivalric love story from this book. Camelot's long literary life begins here.
chretien-cliges-comfort-1914:
Chretien de Troyes wrote Cliges as his second Arthurian romance in the twelfth century. W. W. Comfort translated it into English in 1914. Byzantine intrigue and an answer to the Tristan legend drive its plot.

Young Cliges travels from Constantinople to Arthur's court in Britain. He loves Fenice, who is married to the emperor, his uncle. A feigned death and a hidden tower let the lovers escape scandal briefly. Chretien argues that love should join body and heart in one person. The romance feels more artful and self-aware than his first. Comfort's version keeps the intricate plotting readable for English audiences.
chretien-yvain-comfort-1914:
Chretien de Troyes composed Yvain, the Knight of the Lion, in the twelfth century. W. W. Comfort's 1914 translation carries the beloved romance into English. A magic fountain in the forest starts the knight's troubles.

Yvain defeats the fountain's guardian and marries the dead man's lady, Laudine. Granted a year for tournaments, he overstays and loses her love entirely. Madness drives him naked into the wilderness to live like a beast. A lion he rescues from a serpent becomes his faithful companion. Together they perform rescues that slowly rebuild his honor. Chivalry, wilderness, and second chances fill Chretien's most humane romance here.
chretien-lancelot-comfort-1914:
Chretien de Troyes wrote Lancelot, the Knight of the Cart, in the twelfth century. W. W. Comfort translated the romance into English in 1914. The poem defines courtly love for the whole Arthurian tradition after it.

Queen Guinevere is abducted, and Lancelot pursues her without hesitation. He climbs into a criminal's cart, the deepest shame a knight could accept. Love outranks honor at every turn of his quest. A sword bridge and a reluctant host's son test him further. Chretien left the poem unfinished, and another hand completed it. The forbidden love at Camelot's heart begins in these pages. No Arthurian theme proved more influential afterward.
plos-pone-0004914:
Dongmei Wu and colleagues showed a conserved Shp2 step controls human and mouse embryonic stem cell pluripotency, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Recent studies suggested distinctive properties between human and mouse embryonic stem cells. The team reports that Shp2, a tyrosine phosphatase, plays a shared role in both species. It steers the signals that decide if stem cells stay pluripotent or start to specialize. That shared role bridges an apparent divide in stem cell biology.

Conserved nodes simplify translation between models. Shp2 balances self renewal against specialization. Culture protocols can target shared machinery. Species differences are real but partial. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0005014:
Protected reserves are the main tool for saving the Amazon. Whether they truly work is still debated. Marion Adeney, Norman Christensen and Stuart Pimm tested them in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used fire as their yardstick. In the Amazon, fires are closely linked to deforestation.

Satellite fire data let them compare reserves with unprotected land. Fires burned less inside reserves. That means reserves do hold the line against forest loss. At least they resist fire-driven clearing. The study gives conservation a hard measure of success. It also shows where protection is weakest. Such evidence helps decide where new reserves will do the most good.
plos-pone-0005114:
Optineurin is a busy protein found in all cells. Its production rises with inflammation signals. Cherukuri Sudhakar and colleagues studied how it is regulated in PLOS ONE in 2009. They focused on the alarm factor NF-kappa B. Tumor necrosis factor alpha triggers that alarm. The question was how the two factors relate.

NF-kappa B mediates optineurin's induction by the tumor signal. Optineurin then acts as a negative regulator of NF-kappa B. The alarm builds its own brake. That feedback loop limits inflammation's run. The finding maps a self-limiting circuit. Such circuits fail in chronic inflammatory disease. Knowing the wiring shows where the failure could sit. It also names optineurin as more than a bystander.
plos-pone-0005214:
On Mount Carmel in Israel, two slopes face each other across a small canyon with sharply different climates. One slope is hot and dry, the other cooler and greener, only meters apart. Raz and colleagues surveyed scorpions there, in a site known as Evolution Canyon, in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The survey recorded which scorpion species live on each slope and how the groups differ. Contrasts packed into a tiny area let researchers watch divergence as it happens. Sites like this are natural labs for testing how local conditions split populations apart over time.
plos-pone-0005314:
Animals of the same species cope with stress in different styles, bold or shy, and style shapes how genes respond to challenges. MacKenzie and colleagues showed in PLOS ONE in 2009 that screening for coping style boosts gene expression studies, using common carp as the example.

Fish with different coping styles shifted gene expression in strikingly different ways under the same challenge. Sorting animals by style before analysis sharpens the signal. Ignoring behavior adds noise, so a simple behavioral screen can make expensive gene studies far more powerful. Fish farms and labs both gain from this trick, since calm fish and bold fish do not read as one group. And a mixed group can wash out a real gene effect.
plos-pone-0005914:
Gabriel Lidzbarsky, Tamar Shkolnik, and Eviatar Nevo sampled wild yeast in 2009 from a canyon famous for sharp contrasts in sun and drought. Natural populations face constant environmental stress, and UV radiation is a chief threat to yeast growth. The canyon's two slopes offer a ready-made experiment in adaptation.

Forty-six natural yeast strains from the site were tested for their responses to DNA-damaging agents. Strains from harsher slopes responded differently, evidence of adaptation in the wild. Such natural experiments show evolution's handwriting without lab contrivance. They also stock strain collections with hardy variants for industry.
plos-pone-0006014:
Each person's inner clock runs a touch longer than a day, and the exact length differs by person. Mark Smith, Helen Burgess, Louis Fogg and colleagues asked in 2009 whether it also differs by race. Their PLOS ONE paper measures the endogenous circadian period, the free-running length of the body clock, in different groups.

That length helps set whether someone leans toward mornings or evenings. A group difference, if real, would shape how sleep advice and shift schedules should be tuned. The study treats the clock as a trait that varies across humanity, and it gives sleep medicine hard numbers where guesswork about race and rhythm had stood before.
plos-pone-0006114:
Group B Streptococcus can infect a baby before birth, inside the womb itself. Izabela Sitkiewicz, Nicole Green, Nina Guo and colleagues asked how the germ adapts to that setting in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper maps the transcriptome, the full set of genes switched on, as the bacteria grow in human amniotic fluid.

The fluid is the germ's first home during intrauterine infection, and its growth program there was poorly known. A full gene map shows which tools the bacteria raise to survive the womb. That knowledge can guide both prevention and treatment of infections that end in fetal harm, where time for testing is short.
plos-pone-0006214:
Bacteria pump out unwanted chemicals using large transporter proteins in their membranes. Aurelien Deniaud and colleagues compared two such pumps, CusA and AcrB, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Until recently AcrB was the only member of its family with a solved structure, and it formed crystals under many conditions.

CusA behaved differently, and the authors trace the contrast to how flexible each protein is. Flexibility shapes whether a protein will sit still for crystal imaging. The lesson helps structural biologists plan work on other stubborn membrane proteins. Those structures, in turn, support drug design against resistant bacteria.
plos-pone-0006714:
Arnaud Saimpont, Thierry Pozzo, and Charalambos Papaxanthis tested mental rotation of hands in younger and older adults in PLOS ONE in 2009. Normal aging changes both movement and thinking. Less was known about how aging affects imagining an action. Mental rotation of a hand picture taps that imagination quietly. Twenty young adults and nineteen older adults took part.

Participants judged left and right hands shown at different angles. Performance differences revealed how aging alters implicit motor imagery. Imagined movement shares machinery with real movement. Declines here can hint at wider motor planning problems. The results help separate normal aging from early disease in action simulation.
plos-pone-0006814:
Peter J. M. Van Haastert and Leonard Bosgraaf studied how amoeboid cells search for food in PLOS ONE in 2009. Search strategies decide success in patchy environments. Some animals use special random walks with occasional long runs. Others keep moving in a preferred direction. Starving cells face the same strategic problem at microscopic scale.

Starvation changed the cells' movement pattern. It induced an extension of run lengths, making searches wider. Longer runs help leave exhausted areas for fresh ground. The strategy mirrors optimal foraging ideas from animal ecology. It shows search rules can be tuned by hunger itself, even without a brain.
plos-pone-0006914:
James C. Johnston and colleagues pooled world data on treating multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in PLOS ONE in 2009. Outcomes for this disease are generally poor. Drug-sensitive tuberculosis cures far more reliably. The authors sought overall outcome estimates across studies. They also hunted risk factors tied to poor outcomes.

Their systematic review and meta-analysis combined many treatment cohorts. Pooling clarifies success, failure, and death rates honestly. Risk factors point to patients needing extra support. Programs can use the numbers to set realistic targets. The synthesis is a reference for a disease where every percentage point matters.
plos-pone-0007014:
Bernhard Englitz, Sandra Tolnai, Marei Typlt, and colleagues tested a giant hearing synapse in PLOS ONE in 2009. The synapses of Held are huge nerve junctions in the auditory pathway. They support faithful, rapid hearing signals. They also serve as a model for central synapses in general. Whether their signals can fail was an open question.

The team recorded these synapses in living animals during sound stimulation. That in vivo test is stricter than work in brain slices. Reliability here underpins the timing precision hearing needs. The results help define the limits of even the strongest synapses.
plos-pone-0007114:
Ammar Al-Chalabi, Alexandra Dürr, Nicholas Wood, and colleagues studied a rare brain disease's genetics in PLOS ONE in 2009. Multiple system atrophy is a progressive disorder of movement and body control. It mixes parkinsonism, balance problems, and autonomic failure. Its cause is obscure, but its hallmark is clumps of the protein alpha-synuclein in support cells.

The team tested variants of the alpha-synuclein gene, SNCA. Variants were associated with the disease. A link to the very protein that clumps is a strong lead. It suggests the gene helps set risk, not just supply the raw material of the clumps.
plos-pone-0007214:
Sabyasachi Halder, Masanao Murakami, Subhash C. Verma, and colleagues built a tool to watch early Epstein-Barr virus infection in 2009. The virus is closely linked to many human cancers. Studying its first steps inside cells could reveal weak points for treatment or prevention.

The team made a self-recombining bacterial artificial chromosome carrying the viral genome. They use it to monitor early cellular and viral events in primary B cells. Their PLOS ONE paper describes the system and its use. Virologists get a controlled way to follow infection from its first hours.
plos-pone-0007314:
Cheng-Han Lee, Subbaya Subramanian, Andrew H. Beck, and colleagues profiled microRNAs in ovarian cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. MicroRNAs are tiny non-coding RNAs that block translation of target messages. They have been implicated in the development of many human cancers, including ovarian malignancies in several studies.

High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma is the most common and lethal ovarian cancer subtype. It can occur in women carrying BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, or without them. The authors profile microRNAs in both groups. Their comparison asks whether inherited mutation status leaves a distinct microRNA signature in tumors.
openalex-w2011868814: Balance tests need local versions to work. A 2004 study brought the Berg balance scale to Brazilian Portuguese. The work checked the reliability of scores from the Brazilian adaptation. Two testers helped validate the translation.
openalex-w2016899314: A citation without a paper — the record is bare. This entry, 'Perez and Goarant BMC Microbiology 2010, 10:325,' preserves only a citation to a 2010 BMC Microbiology article. The thin catalog record hides the topic entirely; the reference points to volume 10, article 325.
plos-pone-0006314:
Glioblastoma is the most frequent and most malignant primary brain tumor. Peter Huszthy and colleagues attacked it with suicide gene therapy in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Lab models often lack key features of the human disease, which has slowed translation of new strategies.

A lentiviral vector delivered the suicide gene into cancer stem-like tumor grafts. Treatment drove those invasive grafts into remission in the model. Cancer stem-like cells are thought to regrow tumors after standard therapy. Hitting them directly is the study's central idea, with remission as encouraging evidence.
plos-pone-0009714:
Brain disorders often share symptoms, from anxiety to psychosis, across different diagnoses. Anthony Deo and colleagues proposed a new way to trace those symptoms back to genes. Their analytical framework appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Behavioral symptoms are often harder to map than the diseases themselves.

The method dissects genetic architecture, the pattern of gene effects behind a trait. It aims to link gene patterns with behavioral symptoms seen in neuropsychiatric disorders. A shared framework could show which symptoms share genetic roots. That would help researchers group patients by biology rather than labels alone.
openalex-w2207949614: Why do people walk or bike in some cities but not others? This 2015 study in Environmental Health Perspectives surveys adults in 17 cities across 12 countries, linking perceptions of their neighborhoods — safety, sidewalks, destinations — to whether they walk or cycle for transport. The IPEN project gives city planners cross-country evidence on which street-level changes actually get people moving.
openalex-w2299123914: Muons are among the cleanest signatures physicists have — but only if the detector reconstructs them faithfully. This 2016 paper measures how well ATLAS finds and measures muons in 13 TeV proton-proton collisions: reconstruction efficiency, momentum scale, and resolution, checked against simulations. The efficiency comes out close to 100% across most of the detector, validating a cornerstone of LHC physics.
openalex-w2972679514: Oxitec's genetically modified mosquitoes carry a lethal gene meant to crash wild populations — but do the genes stay put? This 2019 Scientific Reports paper finds transgenic Aedes aegypti transferred genes into a natural population.
