The result complicates the story of engineered mosquito control for yellow fever, dengue, chikungunya, and Zika.
openalex-w3029408214: As coronavirus tore through northern Italy, modelers raced to project its course. This 2020 Frontiers in Public Health paper simulates the epidemic with a deterministic SEIR model, computing infections and casualties. The example shows how simple models informed decisions in the pandemic's early chaos.
europmc-pmc2808214: Antibodies that hit the malaria germ's blood stage might shield children, but proof was thin. This 2010 review pools trials of anti-merozoite antibodies and malaria rates. Punch, volume 146, dated January 28, 1914, finds comedy in diplomacy. The American Ambassador, readers were told last week, has a cold. He is confined to his room at the Embassy by it.

Yufan Xia and three co-authors use learn tools to set thread counts for a core math task. The task is matrix times matrix, the work horse of science code. On one thread, the best tune is well known. On many threads that share RAM, the best count of threads is hard to call. Too few wastes cores. Too many clogs the RAM path.

The team trains a model to call the best thread count for each new task shape. It learns from past runs on like tasks. At run time it sets the count in a flash, with no trial runs. A reader who runs science code gets a way to cut wait time on a task that eats much of world compute.
arxiv-2601-09214:
Jiri Cerny and Flavio Dalessi study the far edge of a branching walk in a chance land. Walkers branch and step on a line of whole points. The land shifts at random from site to site, yet stays fixed once set. The far edge is the most far point a walker has reached. Past work found how that edge tends to sit in a plain land.

In a chance land, they prove the edge law stays tight round its mid point. Tight here means the edge does not spread out with out bound as time grows. That holds for near all lands, not just on mean. A reader in chance work gets a firm tale for a walk where the land itself is a throw of dice.
arxiv-2601-09314:
Gerold Alsmeyer and Anita Behme study the tail of a class of chance flows that pull back to a mean. Such flows model rates, winds, and counts that jump, then drift back. Here the drift rules are set by a hid chain that flips state. Each state has its own pull and jump form. The tail asks how oft a vast value can still show.

They read the tail through a chain of random affine maps. Each map scales and shifts the last value. Tails of such chains have known power forms, with rates set by the maps. A reader in chance work gets a tail law for a flow that can flip its own rules as it runs.
arxiv-2601-09514:
Sagardeep Talukdar, R. Ramakrishnan, Sudipta Nandy, and M. Lakshmanan follow bright pulses as they travel down a flawed fiber. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies soliton dynamics through the variable-coefficient Fokas-Lenells equation. The fiber is inhomogeneous: its dispersion, nonlinearity, and gain or loss change with time.

The authors set up the model for ultrashort pulses in such fibers. They then examine how bright solitons interact, along with conservation laws, modulation instability, and soliton tunneling. Solitons that survive a changing fiber are prized for fast optical links. Knowing when they pass through barriers, or break up, guides fiber design.
arxiv-2601-09614:
Xiang-Xiang Sun and six co-authors compute the electric shape of two light nuclei from first principles. Their 2026 arXiv paper predicts charge form factors and radii for lithium-6 and beryllium-8. The method is the Jacobi-coordinate no-core shell model.

The forces come from chiral two- and three-nucleon interactions, with matching one- and two-nucleon charge operators. Two-body charge terms are the paper's focus: do they matter at this precision? Form factors tell how charge is spread inside a nucleus, and radii give its size. Clean predictions give experiments a theory benchmark with no fitted knobs at all.
arxiv-2601-09914:
Nathaniel Grimes, Christopher Costello, and Andrew Plantinga study fishers and a new form of cover. Fish stocks face shocks from storms and shifts in the sea. These shocks hit both the stock and the pay of those who fish. Index cover pays out when a set index drops, not when one boat has a bad trip.

Such cover could shield fishers from risk. But it may also change how they fish. If cover makes risk feel low, effort may rise. That could add strain to stocks that are prone to over use. The paper weighs this trade off. It urges care in how such plans are set up and rolled out.
arxiv-2601-10314:
Eske Pedersen and co authors pull a faint bias from galaxy shapes in survey data. Galaxies tend to point in ways set by their birth place. That lean can fake the weak lens signal that maps dark mass. The lean is named intrinsic alignment.

The team add a self tune step to a known lens pipe. The pipe is the LSST DESC 3x2pt chain. They run it on year one data from the Dark Energy Survey. The step uses the data itself to split lean from lens. It shows the pipe can do both jobs at once. That bodes well for the vast LSST runs to come.
arxiv-2601-10514:
Madeline Lucey and co authors report the first five carbon rich metal poor stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud. Such stars hold far more carbon than iron for their age. In our own galaxy, they are a large share of old halo stars. They code facts about the first stars and their bursts.

No such stars were known in that dwarf galaxy till now. The team found five. Each is a clue to how the first bursts seeded that galaxy. The mix in a dwarf may part from our own in key ways. The finds give a first base for that match.
arxiv-2601-10614:
Yair Hayut and Alejandro Poveda study the Rudin-Keisler order, a way of ranking ultrafilters on measurable cardinals. Set theorists use such rankings to compare very large infinite sets. The paper asks how directed this order is: can two ultrafilters always be bounded by a third? Their main theorem gives a precise answer in terms of consistency.

For regular cardinals in the stated range, two theories turn out to be equiconsistent with ZFC, the standard axioms of set theory. That means each can be true if the other can. Results like this map the possible shapes of the ultrafilter order. They guide set theorists who probe what large cardinals force and what they leave free.
arxiv-2601-10914:
Francis N. Nji and Jianwu Wang present a factorized-attention ConvLSTM for climate data. Learning useful patterns from high-resolution Earth data is hard. Local weather shifts fast, distant regions sway each other, and the whole system drifts over time. ConvLSTM2D is a common baseline, but its dense gating costs much compute. Its local view also misses long-range structure.

The authors add factorized attention to widen the model's reach while cutting cost. The design aims at physically meaningful space-time patterns across many variables. Climate data are a natural test: teleconnections link oceans and continents. A leaner, wider model could sharpen forecasts and help scientists pull apart tangled climate dynamics.
arxiv-2601-12014:
Elio Masciari, Vincenzo Moscato, Enea Vincenzo Napolitano, and their co-authors test language models on a new structured output format called TOON. Models in pipelines must now give outputs that code can read at once. Good prose is not enough if the form is wrong.

Their test weighs two goals: strict form skill and lasting cost. A format may be cheap yet hard for models to keep valid. Or it may be safe yet waste tokens. The trade map helps teams pick formats for machine-to-machine work with eyes open.  The test also tracks cost per task for each format.
arxiv-2601-12114:
Yikang Lu, Ying Wang, Alfonso de Miguel-Arribas, Lei Shi, and Yamir Moreno model vaccine choice under peer pressure in groups of three. Vaccine games in higher-order settings are still little studied. Yet group pressure shapes views and joint choices in real life.

Their model has two layers. One layer spreads disease by the SIR process on a grid. The other is a hypergraph of triad links where views are pressed. The pair shows how group pressure can lift or sink uptake. Such models can guide fair, peer-led health drives.  Group size in the model is fixed at three peers.
arxiv-2601-12214:
Ahhyun Jeong, Aditya N. Singh, Josh Portner, and a large team align atoms in superlattices of lead sulfide nanocrystals. Nanocrystals are building blocks for new materials, and their self-assembly can yield traits no bulk solid has. The team use compact inorganic ligands on the crystal surfaces.

They reach atomic alignment via reversible oriented attachment, where crystals join and can still adjust. Aligned lattices can carry charge and light in new ways. The work shows a route to ordered films with atomic registry. Such films suit sensors and solar tools.  Atomic registry is the main gain over past films.
arxiv-2601-12314:
Yiwen Zhang, Hui Zhang, and Fanqin Meng link musical structure to military strategy via a similarity network. Music perception is a multi-sense act tied to synesthesia, and it is a core part of music aesthetic education. Grasping music structure aids both perception and teaching.

In music, many strands of information join to form a melody. In strategy, many acts join to form a plan. Their network maps likeness between the two kinds of structure. That odd link may give new tools for music teaching.  The link is drawn for use in aesthetic education.
arxiv-2601-11214:
Hanchen Xia, Baoyou Chen, Yutang Ge, Guojiang Zhao, and Siyu Zhu train diffusion language models. Their 2026 preprint names its method T-star, built on TraceRL. Masked diffusion models write text by filling blanks in blocks. Block size sets a trade-off between speed and quality of the text.

The team's plan grows the block size in steps during training. It starts from a small-block model first trained in the standard way. Then it moves to larger blocks in a smooth path. Larger blocks let the model decode more text in parallel. Tests on math reasoning tasks show small loss of quality. The gain is faster decoding with far more done at once.
arxiv-2601-11314:
Jiatong Yi and Yanyang Li test membership attacks on language models in the wild. Their 2026 preprint deals with large language models as found in use. A membership attack asks if one text trained the model. That test audits what opaque training sets truly held.

Most past tests lean on things users cannot see. Logits and other internals are hid by real services. In a strict black-box case, only the output text shows. Tests also tend to fail when the domain shifts. The team's work targets that real-world black-box case. It aims at an audit tool that needs no inside access. Such a tool helps check privacy and copyright claims.
arxiv-2601-11514:
Yawar Siddiqui and seven coauthors rebuild 3D shapes from casual captures. Their 2026 preprint presents ShapeR, a conditional generation method. Recent 3D generation methods post strong results on clean inputs. Clean means unoccluded and well segmented from the start.

Real captures rarely meet those tidy conditions at all. Phones grab cluttered scenes with parts hidden from view. ShapeR takes casually captured sequences as its input. It generates the object's full 3D shape from them. The conditioning comes from the messy footage itself. Robust shape tools serve scanning, retail, and robot work. The method aims to close the lab-to-life gap.
arxiv-2601-13114:
Abdelrahman Soliman, Ahmed Refaey, Aiman Erbad, and Amr Mohamed build a smart agent for next gen mobile nets. Such nets aim to run by intent. An operator states what the net should do, in plain high level terms, and tools make it so.

Their agent is called IntAgent. It is built on a large language model. It draws on NWDAF, the net data analytics role in 5G cores, plus a set of tools. With that mix it can read net state and act to meet an intent. For net teams, the work shows how language agents may cut hand work in day to day net care.
arxiv-2601-13514:
Ronan Perry, Snigdha Panigrahi, and Daniela Witten do post pick inference for penalized M estimators by score thinning. An M estimator fits a model by a loss sum. A sparsity penalty picks which parts stay. Inference past that pick is hard, since the pick used the same data.

Old routes need a bespoke proof for each penalty. Their route is more plain. They add and take a crafted noise from a Gaussian count. That split yields two free Gaussian counts. One can drive the pick. The next can drive a plain trust span past the pick. A shared trick for many penalties beats a new proof per task.
arxiv-2601-12414:
Nawaf Mohammed compares two classic ways to measure spread in a set of risks. One is the standard deviation, taught in every basic stats course. The other is the Gini mean difference, less known but widely used in economics. A natural question is which of the two tends to be larger, and when.

Mohammed drives the whole analysis with one structural object. That object is the mean excess function of the gap between two draws of the same risk. The tail of that gap turns out to govern the order of the two measures. Work of this kind helps users know what each spread measure is really picking up. It also warns when the two can rank the same risks in opposite ways.
arxiv-2601-12514:
Graph total colorings get extended to cell complexes in work that links coloring with domination. A total coloring paints both the vertices and the edges of a graph. It is called efficient when each color class forms an efficient dominating set on the vertices. Efficient domination is a strict form of coverage with no overlap or waste.

The focus falls on two cell complexes whose one dimensional skeletons are toroidal graphs. Toroidal graphs live on a doughnut shaped surface, which gives them a rich, regular structure. Extending coloring ideas from graphs to complexes tests how far the concepts stretch. Results here sit in combinatorics and topology at once. The author line in the record is blank, so no creator is named here.
arxiv-2601-12614:
Neural surrogates for global space plasma simulations are built in work with no author named in the record. The target simulations use a hybrid Vlasov method that resolves ion kinetic effects. They model how the solar wind interacts with the magnetosphere of Earth. Even reduced five dimensional runs of this kind are very expensive to compute.

The team train graph based machine learning emulators on four such runs. All four runs use identical steady solar wind conditions. The emulators learn how fields and ion moments evolve in near Earth space. Both deterministic and probabilistic surrogates are built and compared. A fast surrogate could let researchers scan many scenarios that full runs cannot afford.
arxiv-2601-13614:
Bo Peng, Sirui Chen, Lei Xu, and Chaochao Lu study how machines can find cause and effect in data in 2026. Pure data methods can stall, since two causes may look the same in the numbers. Newer methods ask large language models for help with cause hunts. But some ignore the data proof, and others trust model guesses that no one has checked.

Their system, CauScientist, aims to make models respect the data first. Model ideas must face the stats proof found in the data itself. The goal is cause claims that stay tied to what was seen. Sound cause work backs both science and hard choices in real life.
arxiv-2601-13914:
Lars Georg, Robert Harlander, and Robert Mason compute a coupling in quantum electrodynamics with a new scheme in 2026. The gradient-flow scheme defines the QED coupling in a smooth, flow-based way. They evaluate it in three and four space-time dimensions. Their general result applies to any theory with a U(1) gauge field.

Other fields and arbitrary interactions are allowed in the result. As an example, they treat QED with a set number of flavors. They evaluate the beta functions, which show how the coupling runs with energy. Such results test field theory methods across dimensions.
arxiv-2601-14114:
Liam Chung and Tobias Kappé extend a logic for reasoning about programs in 2026. Kleene algebra is a tool for proving general program equivalences. Its equational theory is decidable and complete. Yet it cannot always prove equivalences between specific programs.

For those cases, users add hypotheses that encode program-specific knowledge. Linear hypotheses are the focus of this work. The team studies partial reductions for Kleene algebra with such hypotheses. Better tools here help verify compilers and program transformations with proof. The cuts keep proofs short while the added facts stay in view. Tool builders can add these cuts to their own provers.
arxiv-2601-14214:
Julia Venturini and co-authors build a global formation model for planets in binaries in 2026. Binary stars are as common as single stars in the galaxy. The number of detected planets orbiting binaries is rapidly increasing. Transit surveys, Gaia, and high-resolution direct imaging campaigns drive that synergy.

Global planet formation models around binary stars are still underdeveloped. That gap limits theoretical understanding of planets in binary systems. Their PAIRS project aims to close the gap with a global model. Observers need such models to interpret the growing census of two-sun worlds.
arxiv-2601-14614:
Víctor Mayoral-Vilches leads a large team on AI in cybersecurity in this 2026 paper. They define cybersecurity superintelligence as artificial intelligence exceeding the best human capability in both speed and strategic reasoning. They call it the next frontier in security. The paper documents the emergence of such capability through three major contributions that pioneered AI Security.

The first contribution they name is PentestGPT from 2023. It established LLM-guided penetration testing. The paper's title traces a shift: from AI-guided humans to human-guided AI. The tone is bold. The team claims a new age is here, and they lay out the proof step by step. Readers get a field history and a claim about where the balance of initiative between analyst and machine now sits.
arxiv-2601-15514:
Shome Chakraborty asks whether broad economic signals can help forecast public health capacity in a 2026 arXiv paper. Economic conditions shape the setting in which health systems work. Yet no one had checked in a systematic way whether they act as leading signals. That gap is what the study takes up. The question is practical: can today's economic data hint at tomorrow's strain?

Chakraborty tests a set of macroeconomic indicators for useful signal. The targets are all tied to capacity. They include jobs in the health and social assistance workforce. They include new business applications in that sector. They also include spending on health care construction. If such links hold, planners gain an early-warning tool. Forecasts could draw on data that already arrives fast and often.
arxiv-2601-15714:
Ryoma Sato proposes a strict yardstick for language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. He calls it the Zero-Error Horizon. It is the maximum range over which a model solves tasks with no errors at all. Averages can hide rare slips. The horizon exposes them: one slip ends the run. Sato argues that this simple measure yields rich insight. He tests it on state-of-the-art models.

His example is pointed. Even GPT-5.2, he reports, fails at counting to five under his test. The title uses that failure as a warning. Trustworthy use needs error-free stretches, not just high average scores. A surgeon-grade tool must be right every time in its working range. The horizon frames exactly how far that range extends for each model.
arxiv-2601-15814:
Ryosuke Yamano and Tetsuo Shibuya improve an algorithm for genome-style string problems in a 2026 arXiv paper. The shortest common superstring problem asks for one short string. It must contain each given string as a substring. A variant adds reverse complements. For each input, either the string or its reverse complement must appear. That variant arises naturally in bioinformatics, where DNA strands come in both orientations.

The authors improve approximation ratios for this variant. An approximation ratio bounds how far a fast method can stray from optimal. Better ratios mean shorter superstrings, found with guarantees. Genome assembly leans on such problems. Reads must be merged into longer sequences with little waste. Sharper guarantees help assemblers promise more about their output.
arxiv-2601-15014:
Michelle Ching, Ioana Popescu, and co-authors study how transformers learn a task from the prompt itself. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with in-context learning for nonparametric regression. The unknown curve is only assumed to be smooth, in the Hölder sense, with no fixed formula.

In-context learning means the model adapts from examples shown to it, with no new training. The authors ask how well a transformer can fit such curves this way. Their results are of the efficient and minimax-optimal kind. That means no method can do much better in the worst case.
arxiv-2601-15114:
Valerio La Gatta, Gian Marco Orlando, and co-authors give simulated social media users more lifelike habits. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with generative agent-based models. Large language models drive agents that mimic people on social platforms.

Such models can show how posts spread and how influence flows. But most agents are defined by demographics, personality traits, and interests alone. They lack behavioral traits, the leanings that shape how a person acts on a platform. So all agents engage in much the same way. The authors add those missing behavior traits to the agents.
arxiv-2601-15214:
Yoshiki Nakamura completes a logic for a common tool in computing. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with regular expressions with lookahead, a pattern language used to match text. Reasoning about when two such patterns match the same text needs firm rules.

Nakamura gives an axiomatic account of that reasoning. He covers both plain language equivalence and the largest substitution-closed equivalence that stays sound. His route uses a variant of propositional dynamic logic on finite linear orders. Two extra operators restrict a stated relation to the identity or else to its complement.
arxiv-2601-16014:
Eder Baron-Prada, Adolfo Anta and Florian Dörfler study how to test if a power grid stays stable. Their 2026 preprint looks at grids where much of the power now comes through grid tied converters. Old checks can be slow and hard to use. The team uses Scaled Relative Graphs, a graph tool, to split the grid part and the converter part apart.

By split, the authors mean each part can be checked on its own. The checks then join to show if the whole loop stays stable. The method works for both linear loads and loads that do not act in a straight line way. That breadth helps grid teams who must plan for real loads. It gives them a fast and clear way to judge new converter setups.
arxiv-2601-16114:
Alex Plyukhin asks if a known noise form is in fact not needed. His 2026 preprint deals with the broad Langevin maths for systems with drag. Tests of that maths oft use a set noise form. They check if long time ends match true rest states. The noise in his study is heat noise from in the system. Its form is not the bell curve form.

Plyukhin shows the maths can hold true with this noise form. Yet he argues the extra form adds no new use. The same ends can be reached with the plain form. That claim trims need less parts from the theory. The work is a close read of what the maths needs.
arxiv-2601-16414:
John Wu and coauthors set out PyHealth 2.0, a tool kit for ward deep learning. Their 2026 preprint deals with blocks that slow ward AI work. Blocks span hard base lines, high compute cost and need for deep ward facts. The kit aims to cut all three blocks at once. It claims a full model can be built in just a few lines.

Few line builds let more teams test ward task ideas fast. Shared base lines make scores fair to weigh side by side. Low cost paths open ward AI to small teams and schools. The kit is free and open for all to use. It builds on the first PyHealth set of tools.
arxiv-2601-17114:
Heng-Yu Chen, Nick Dorey, Sanefumi Moriyama, Rishi Mouland, and Canberk Şanlı tie two brane tales in one claim. M2 and M5 branes are vast sheets in M-theory. Each hosts its own field tale on its face. Their 2026 preprint claims a tight link twixt two such tales. One tale is the ABJM tale in three dims. It rules stacks of M2 branes in flat space-time.

Count marks, called indices, are the link's test. A giant graviton growth gives one side of the tie. If the tie holds, counts in one tale fix the next. Such dual ties are gold in string work.
arxiv-2601-17514:
Nitin Jha and Abhishek Parakh survey if quantum voting can work in practice. Quantum voting aims for ballot secrecy with public proof of the tally. Its shield rests on physics, not just hard math. Superposition, no-cloning, and entanglement are the core tools. The authors weigh those promises against real-world needs.

Elections demand scale, ease of use, and trust by non-experts. A scheme can be sound in theory and fail at the polls. The survey maps that gap in plain terms. It helps officials judge claims from quantum vendors. It also shows researchers which flaws to fix first. Ballot trust is too key to rest on lab demos.
arxiv-2601-17614:
Yimeng Liu, Misha Sra, and Chang Xiao present AlignUI for interface design with language models. Good interfaces match user taste, but finding that match takes long cycles. Teams prototype, test, and refine again and again. LLM-based UI generation speeds the build phase. AlignUI aims to steer that speed toward user preference.

A fast tool that misses taste saves little time. Alignment methods close the gap between first draft and fit. Designers can explore more options in the same span. Users gain screens shaped to their habits. The work joins generation with feedback in one loop. It serves product teams under real deadlines.
arxiv-2601-17914:
Casper Vedder, Thomas Bakx, Nora Elisa Chisari, Henk Hoekstra, and Matthieu Schaller measure a subtle effect in how galaxies line up. Their 2026 preprint uses the FLAMINGO simulations, a large set of virtual universes. Galaxies and their dark matter halos tend to align with the web around them. These intrinsic alignments can mimic the lensing signal that cosmologists use to weigh the universe, so they must be modeled with care.

The team goes past pairs and measures three-point statistics. They compute a three-point correlation and a third-order aperture-mass measure. The sample covers galaxies and halos above a set mass in a huge simulated volume. Three-point data add checks that pair data cannot give. The results help lensing surveys clean their signals.
arxiv-2601-18014:
Adeeba Tarannum and co-authors build a system that turns messy name and address text into clean fields. Their 2026 preprint targets a basic pain in large information systems. Free text must be split into parts like first name, street, and city before it can be used. Rule-based and statistical tools do well on clean input but fail on noisy or multilingual text. Neural models and language models, in turn, can lack steady control and repeatability.

The team's system uses large language models with those flaws in mind. Steady output matters when records feed billing, shipping, and identity checks. Better parsing cuts errors across huge record sets. The work serves any group that cleans contact data at scale.
arxiv-2601-18314:
Lina Felsner and co-authors report a student hackathon built around reproducing MRI results. Their 2026 preprint describes the design, protocol, and outcomes of the event. Students set out to replicate three influential MRI reconstruction papers. One is MoDL, an unrolled model-based network with learned denoising. The second is HUMUS-Net, a hybrid unrolled design that mixes CNN and transformer parts. The third is an untrained, physics-regularized method for dynamic MRI that uses a quantitative prior.

Reproduction is a hard test of whether a paper gives enough detail to rebuild its claims. A hackathon format turns that test into training. The outcomes show where advanced methods stand up to fresh hands. Such exercises strengthen the field's habits of care.
arxiv-2601-19714:
G. Lacopo and four colleagues speed up the imaging software behind radio astronomy. Modern radio interferometers pour out enormous data volumes. Turning those measurements into sky images is a heavy computation. The coming SKA telescopes will dwarf today's instruments, so the pipelines must scale.

The team presents RICK 2.0, a new version of their radio imaging code. It uses a library for distributed Fourier transforms, the mathematical heart of the imaging step. The design aims at high performance that still ports across different supercomputers. Tests use data from precursors of the SKA telescopes. Faster, portable imaging is a precondition for the science those telescopes promise.
arxiv-2601-19814:
Marco Antonio Rosas Pulido and colleagues propose a new way to describe a city's economy. A city's firms, institutions, and spatial layout interact in intricate ways. Standard measures of economic complexity lean on what a city exports. The authors instead build a framework from three structural dimensions of economic units: abundance, diversity, and longevity.

Abundance counts how many units exist, diversity how varied they are, and longevity how long they last. Together these serve as proxies for complexity and resilience. A city strong on all three should weather shocks better. The framework gives planners a fresh lens on urban economies. It can be computed from firm-level records many cities already keep.
arxiv-2601-19914:
Maxwell Crouse and four colleagues build training data for AI agents that call tools. Synthetic data can teach smaller, cheaper models to handle multi-turn tool conversations. Many frameworks for making such data assume the tools run in a stateful environment. That environment remembers earlier calls and their effects.

Real deployments often run tools statelessly, with no memory between calls. The authors simulate complex multi-turn interactions inside such stateless execution environments. Their simulations must carry the needed context in the conversation itself. Training on data that matches the deployment setting should transfer better. The work closes a quiet mismatch between how agent data is made and how agents actually run.
arxiv-2601-20114:
J. N. Bai and four colleagues propose a way to build an exotic quantum model inside an array of Rydberg atoms. The target is the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, a chain model known for skin effects, where states pile up at one edge. Their setup uses a chain of atoms with three atoms in each unit cell.

A synthetic gauge field is made by shining multi-color laser fields on the atoms. Each atom can be addressed on its own, which gives fine control over the chain. The scheme offers a clean lab test bed for non-Hermitian physics, where loss and gain are part of the model rather than a flaw.
arxiv-2601-18714:
Judith Vilella-Cantos and four colleagues teach farm robots to know where they are in a field of vines. A vine field is a hard place to get one's place. Rows look the same, there are few firm marks, and leaves shift with the wind and the year. Tools that work in towns, with their signs and walls, fail in such sameness. Place tools for farms have lagged those for roads.

The team use a beam tool that reads range by light. They teach it codes for each place that nest like dolls, from broad to fine. A nest of codes can be both small to store and sharp to match. A cheap, firm place read could let farm robots run rows on their own. That would cut hand work in a trade short of hands.
arxiv-2601-21414:
Chenxu Yang and eight co-authors blend fast gut-level replies with slow careful reasoning in one language model. Human thought is often split into a quick intuitive mode and a slow deliberate one. Training a single model to switch between the two modes runs into clashes between them.

Earlier fixes mostly capped what the slow mode could output. The authors instead blend the two modes by mixing the models themselves, with the mix shifting as needed. Dynamic blending lets the system stay quick on easy items and slow down when a task demands care. That balance is key for cheap, reliable AI help.
arxiv-2601-21714:
A memory system for language model agents rebuilds past episodes in full context instead of compressing them. Long, careful problem solving needs memory that stays faithful over long spans. Most current memory tools squeeze past events into embeddings or graphs before storing them.

That squeezing cuts the context that gives each event its meaning. The authors' multi-agent design reconstructs episodes with their sequential links intact. Keeping context whole should support deeper reasoning across long tasks. The work targets agents that must stay coherent over hours of work, where a mangled memory can quietly wreck the whole chain.
arxiv-2601-22314:
Gyu Whan Chang and Giulio Peruginelli give a full account of a family of rings that sit between two classic polynomial rings. Their 2026 preprint studies domains — number systems with no zero divisors — that are integrally closed and Noetherian. The family lies between integer and rational polynomial rings in one variable.

The team sort the family by sorting the Krull domains inside it. A complete map of this kind closes a gap in ring theory. It gives algebra scholars a firm base for nearby questions. The work is pure math, with no device in view. Its value is the finished map itself.
arxiv-2601-22614:
Shyam Venkatasubramanian and a team steady transformer training with a consensus rule. Standard attention models can go unstable when the learning rate is set too high. Their 2026 preprint notes that most fixes tweak the optimizer, while the architecture itself stays untouched.

Their consensus step acts inside the model to curb that instability. Stable training at bold rates would cut tuning time and failed runs. It matters most for huge models, where one bad run costs a fortune. The work is an architectural answer to a training pain. It aims for calm by design.
arxiv-2601-22714:
Alexander Nikulin and four co-authors use vision-language models to teach latent action models what counts as a real action. Latent action models learn action codes from video, and feed the training of robot-ready systems. Their 2026 preprint notes that they fail when the scene holds distractors that move with the action.

People split true motion from noise at a glance; the team give models that task sense. Cleaner action codes should yield robots that learn faster from video. The work links language-guided vision to robot skill. It fixes a subtle, common flaw.
arxiv-2601-21814:
Eduard Paul Enoiu, Jean Malm, and Gregory Gay argue that software teams run partly on folklore. They mean the stories, myths, rituals, jokes, and informal know-how that circulate inside development communities and shape how people actually work. Their 2026 paper sets out to define this idea properly for software engineering.

Drawing on folklore studies, the authors use a literature review and thematic analysis to characterize the concept. They gather example items. These include beliefs about where defects tend to occur. They also include the legend of the developer who is ten times better than peers. Naming this folklore matters because unwritten beliefs guide real choices about process, hiring, and quality, whether teams admit it or not.
arxiv-2601-21914:
Zhouyou Gu, Jihong Park, and Jinho Choi plan links inside vast constellations of low Earth orbit satellites. Laser links between satellites offer high-capacity, long-range connections that can make these networks resilient. Planning them well is harder than it first looks.

Existing schemes often ignore the mechanical limits of laser terminals, which must physically aim, and the uneven traffic demands around the globe. The team's 2026 preprint jointly handles link matching and traffic routing, using Lagrangian decomposition to split the big problem into solvable parts. Better link planning means more usable bandwidth from the same satellites, which affects the cost and quality of global satellite internet.
arxiv-2601-22014:
B. D. Lailey and T. A. A. Sigut check whether the standard ways of finding Be stars are biased by viewing angle. Be stars are fast-spinning stars with disks of gas around them. Whether we look at such a system nearly edge-on or nearly pole-on is its inclination, and it changes what we see.

The authors review several identification methods for bias with respect to inclination. They focus on two photometric methods that use narrow-band filters centered on the hydrogen alpha line. And one spectroscopic method that hunts for peaks in that line. Their 2026 preprint matters because biased catalogs distort everything built on them, from how common Be stars are to how their disks evolve.
arxiv-2601-20714:
Raul de la Rosa, Ivana Dusparic, and Nicolas Cardozo study learning agents that must cope with change. Their 2026 paper is about reinforcement learning, where an agent learns by trial and reward. In the real world, the rules of the game can shift mid-task. Rewards may change, or new actions may open up. Most agents handle such shifts poorly.

The team presents morphin, a self-adaptive form of Q-learning. Q-learning is a classic method where an agent learns the value of each action. Morphin adjusts on the fly when the action set or rewards change. It does so without full retraining from scratch. The paper speaks to anyone who needs agents that keep working when their world will not sit still.
arxiv-2601-20914:
Nicolás Cardiel and six co-authors built a Python package to teach a core astronomy skill. Their 2026 paper presents teareduce. The package supports teaching the reduction of astronomical data. Reduction is the step that turns raw telescope output into clean, usable images. The package serves students in practical classes. Their courses process images from various instruments and telescopes.

Good teaching tools must be simple but honest. Teareduce gives students utilities that mirror real workflows. They can learn calibration and cleaning steps on actual data. The authors are astronomers and educators sharing their classroom material. Open teaching code helps other schools run the same practicals. The paper is a resource note for anyone who trains new observers.
arxiv-2601-21014:
Haixiang Sun and five co-authors make causal discovery cheaper by thinking locally. Their 2026 paper presents VISTA, a framework for learning causal structures from observational data. The task is fundamental but computationally intensive. In high dimensions, the search space grows super-exponentially. Existing methods strain under the load. VISTA answers with modular subgraph integration, as its full name spells out.

The framework splits the global problem into local subgraphs. Each subgraph is built from Markov blankets, the small sets that screen off each variable. Local structures are learned separately, then merged. A voting step integrates the pieces into one acyclic graph. Modularity keeps the cost in check as data grow. The method serves scientists who need causal maps from big, passive datasets.
arxiv-2512-01314:
Pei Yang and co-authors build a tool that strips hidden marks from images. Hidden marks, or watermarks, prove who owns a file. They guard art, photos, and AI-made work from theft. A mark that is easy to strip gives weak proof.

Their tool, TokenPure, tests how strong those marks are. It uses a diffusion model to clean an image while keeping its look. The tool splits the image into parts for form and parts for look. That split helps it erase the mark with less harm. Weak marks found this way push makers to build stronger ones.
arxiv-2512-01614:
Armen Asratian and Carl Johan Casselgren study an edge coloring transform index for graphs. Edge coloring paints edges so touching edges differ. The transform index is the least steps to turn any valid coloring into any other. Steps recolor one edge at a time while staying valid.

That index tells how flexible a coloring system is. Low values mean colorings can be reshaped with ease. The work builds theory for that index across graphs. Flexible recoloring matters for scheduling and network tasks where colors must shift without breaking rules. Recoloring steps mirror live network upkeep, where links change class as loads shift but service rules must hold at every step between.
arxiv-2512-01014:
Ajneet Dhillon, Nicole Lemire, Jonathan Martin, and Yidi Wang study approximation for classifying stacks in a 2025 math paper. A classifying stack packages all the ways a group can act into a single geometric object. Strong approximation asks whether solutions over local data can be glued into a global one.

The Brauer-Manin obstruction is a known test that can block such gluing. The authors prove that its étale version is the only obstruction to strong approximation for these stacks. The result holds when the group is linear algebraic over a number field. A single complete test simplifies a hard existence question across arithmetic geometry.
arxiv-2512-01114:
Yukinari Sumino proposes a way to measure a bound quark system's wave function in a 2025 physics paper. The wave function of quarkonium, a heavy quark bound to its antiquark, is defined inside potential nonrelativistic QCD, an effective theory for such systems. Until now it had no direct experimental probe.

Sumino uses the three-body decay of the Bc meson, which contains both a bottom and a charm quark. He shows the momentum distribution of the spectator charm quark mirrors the squared wave function of the parent state. If measured, this would be the first experimental handle on a quantity long treated as theory-only.
arxiv-2512-01214:
Hang Wu and five coauthors improve detection of manipulated media in a 2025 paper. Multimodal manipulation, where images, audio, and text are faked together, threatens the reliability of information people receive. Current detection methods often overlook localized information, even though manipulations usually occur in specific areas, especially facial regions.

Their system, M4-BLIP, adds face-enhanced local analysis to a multimodal model. By inspecting faces and other local regions closely, it hunts for the small inconsistencies that global checks miss. Better local detection could help platforms and journalists flag deepfakes that look convincing at a glance.
arxiv-2601-22914:
Fabrizio Canfora and three co-authors find exact black hole solutions with uneven, bumpy horizons. The solutions come from Einstein's equations joined with a model of superfluid pions, a kind of matter field. Their setup uses spinning pion patterns arranged as many vortices.

With that pattern, the matter equations shrink to a simpler first-order system. The gravity side becomes a known equation whose source shapes the horizon's bumps. Exact solutions are rare in gravity, and they give clean tests for theories of black holes and dense matter. Bumpy horizons stretch the usual picture of black holes as smooth spheres, showing how matter fields can deform them.
arxiv-2601-23014:
Yanwei Yue and co-authors train memory agents that manage their own memories. Unlike fixed pipelines, these agents decide how to process, store, and fetch what they learn. Training them is hard because rewards arrive sparsely, only after long chains of memory operations.

Their method, Mem-T, densifies those rewards so learning signals come more often. Denser feedback makes end-to-end training of memory policy practical. Agents with well-managed memory could handle long projects without forgetting key facts. Densifying rewards means the agent no longer waits through long memory-operation chains for a single delayed training signal. Earlier paradigms left agents wandering such chains with almost no feedback, which stalled end-to-end learning of memory policy.
arxiv-2512-00114:
The neutron skin of a nucleus is the thin layer where neutrons extend beyond the protons. Andreas Vitsos, Leonora Misciattelli Mocenigo Soranzo, and You Zhou study the skin of calcium-48 in a 2025 article. Their evidence comes from collective flow in collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider.

The team uses a method nicknamed imaging by smashing. It links the flow of debris from ultra-relativistic collisions back to the structure of the colliding nuclei. Most earlier work targeted nuclear shape, such as deformation, rather than skin thickness. Measuring the skin helps test nuclear models and connects to the physics of neutron stars. The findings feed into wider efforts to pin down how neutrons arrange themselves in heavy nuclei.
arxiv-2512-00214:
Grammar research increasingly runs on large annotated text collections, yet analyzing them still takes heavy technical effort. A 2025 study examines how agentic large language models could streamline that work across languages. The models reason over annotated corpora instead of single example sentences.

The goal is interpretable, data-grounded answers to linguistic questions, produced with less manual setup. Corpus-grounded agents could help linguists test claims about grammar against real usage at scale. The study speaks to a wider shift in the humanities, where language models are becoming research assistants rather than just text generators. Multilingual coverage matters because grammar traditions and corpora differ sharply across languages. The authors explore the approach rather than claim a finished system.
arxiv-2512-00314:
Counting the traces a formal language can produce is a basic question in theoretical computer science. Alexis de Colnet, Kuldeep Meel, and Umang Mathur study counting and sampling traces in regular languages in 2025. Traces account for which actions can run independently and commute.

The setup fixes an alphabet with an independence relation, a regular language given by a finite automaton, and a length given in unary. Counting and sampling underpin verification of concurrent systems, where independent actions interleave freely. The work clarifies how hard these problems are, guiding tool builders who model real concurrent software. Regular languages are the simplest language class, which makes the hardness results sharper.
arxiv-2512-00614:
Multi-agent systems let language-model agents work as a team with no central controller. Goutham Nalagatla extends AgentNet in 2025 with hierarchical coordination and privacy-preserving knowledge sharing, aiming at scalable autonomous systems. AgentNet showed fully decentralized coordination through dynamic directed acyclic graph topologies.

Limitations remain: scalability with large agent populations, message overhead, missing privacy guarantees, and weak use of shared compute. The extension attacks those gaps with hierarchy and protected sharing. As agent groups grow, coordination that preserves privacy becomes a must for use in business and public systems. Hierarchy gives the coordinator-free system a way to organize very large agent groups. Privacy-preserving sharing lets agents cooperate without exposing their raw knowledge. For firms that plan fleets of such aides, the gain is a way to grow. More aides can join, share what they know, and still keep each firm's facts safe.
arxiv-2512-03414:
Fluid with tiny particles flows differently near a flat plate. Christian Thomas, Sharon Stephen, Jitesh Gajjar, and Paul Griffiths study that flow's stability in this 2025 work. They examine a nanofluid boundary layer, the thin zone where flow meets the surface.

Their two-phase model includes Brownian motion and thermophoresis, two effects that move small particles. It builds on earlier work in the field. Stability analysis shows when smooth flow breaks into disturbances. Such knowledge helps design cooling and coating systems that use nanofluids. Particle motion effects can trigger instability earlier than a simple fluid model predicts.
arxiv-2512-01914:
Rooftop solar panels and electric vehicles are reshaping how buildings draw power, hour by hour, in ways grid operators struggle to predict. Aiko Fias, Md Umar Hashmi, and Geert Deconinck compare methods in 2025 for quantifying that uncertainty in net electricity load profiles.

They study three building types, homes, industrial sites, and offices, under growing adoption of solar generation and vehicle charging. The question is which metrics honestly capture the spread of possible loads at the local distribution level. Choosing the right measure matters, because planners size equipment and set prices around these uncertain forecasts.
arxiv-2512-02014:
Most AI systems either understand images or generate them, and unified models try to do both in one framework. Zhiheng Liu and a large team present Tuna in 2025, a native unified multimodal model built around a single continuous representation of visual content.

Tuna cascades two encoders: a variational autoencoder that compresses images, and a representation encoder that adds meaning. The shared representation space then serves both understanding and generation, for images and video alike, processed end to end. A common visual language inside the model could make its two talents reinforce rather than compete with each other.
arxiv-2512-02214:
Reinforcement learning agents come in many configurations, and picking the wrong one wastes training. Aida Afshar and Aldo Pacchiano study in 2025 online model selection: a selector that watches a class of learning agents during training and adaptively picks the configuration that is performing best.

The aim is to show improved efficiency and performance from weaving selection into the training procedure itself, rather than tuning beforehand by trial and error. Good selection adapts as learning progresses, since the best configuration early may not stay best. Their results matter for practitioners who cannot afford to train every variant of an agent to completion.
arxiv-2512-02314:
The Alexander polynomial of a knot-like link encodes its crossings in a list of coefficients. Fox conjectured in 1962 that for alternating links, those coefficients rise and then fall like a trapezoid. Karola Mészáros, Melissa Sherman-Bennett, and Alexander Vidinas attack the conjecture in 2025 from an unexpected side: dimers.

Dimers are pairings of adjacent points, a statistical mechanics staple, and the authors build a dimer model whose counts mirror the polynomial's coefficients. Special cases of the conjecture have fallen recently, including special alternating links, but the general statement remains open. A dimer viewpoint could supply the combinatorial grip that direct knot theory has lacked.
arxiv-2512-02414:
Satellites and ground stations have been attacked since at least 1977, when a transmission signal was hijacked, yet no single dataset records these incidents properly. Ekzhin Ear and five co-authors build in 2025 a framework for characterizing cyber attacks against space infrastructure when much of the data are missing.

Reports of such attacks are scattered across media stories with many details absent, so the framework is designed for incomplete evidence. Their case study shows how characterization can proceed anyway. As space systems become critical infrastructure, understanding their attack history is a prerequisite for defending them, even when the record is patchy.
arxiv-2512-02714:
Mohsen Fathi, Ariel Guzmán, and J.R. Villanueva compute the fading tones of a black hole in a modified theory of electromagnetism. Quasinormal modes are the characteristic vibrations a disturbed black hole rings with as it settles. Their hole is static, sits in anti-de Sitter space, and is sourced by a Plebański type nonlinear electrodynamics model.

The authors study axial electromagnetic modes, setting waves to fall into the horizon and vanish suitably at the boundary. Mode frequencies test both the hole and the modified theory. Such catalogs guide future comparisons with gravitational wave data. Each tone in the list is a test the next wave of finds can check as new holes are heard to ring.
arxiv-2512-02914:
Zhonghao He and three co-authors grade language models on whether longer reasoning actually tracks truth. Reasoning methods have lifted model performance, raising hopes for accurate, reliable answers. Yet emerging evidence suggests step by step reasoning can entrench early beliefs instead of correcting them.

Their Martingale Score is an unsupervised metric for Bayesian rationality in model reasoning. It checks whether belief updates behave as honest probability updates should. A cheap truth tracking metric could flag models that sound more certain the longer they talk, without becoming more right. A score that needs no gold set can be run each week. That is how drift gets caught while it is still small and cheap to fix.
arxiv-2512-03014:
Matthew Dutson and three co-authors adapt still image models for video without letting outputs flicker. Frame based networks applied one frame at a time often show temporal inconsistency. Time varying corruptions in the input make the flicker worse, as each frame is cleaned differently.

Their Instant Video Models act as universal adapters for image based networks. The adapters stabilize inference and add robustness across the video. One adapter for many models saves retraining each network for video, a gain for restoration, enhancement, and analysis tools that now work frame by frame. One wrap for many tools is a thrift that counts. Each tool would else need weeks of new work to run on film at a fair rate of speed.
plos-pone-0010014:
Derya Shimshek, Matthias Mueller, Christoph Wiessner, and co-workers tested a hoped-for Parkinson's treatment in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. In Parkinson's disease, a protein called alpha-synuclein folds badly and clumps in the brain. Heat-shock proteins help refold proteins or clear them away, so they looked like a natural way to cut that clump load.

The team raised levels of the chaperone HSP70 in a mouse model of alpha-synuclein disease. Their title gives the plain result: HSP70 was not beneficial there. A clear negative finding like that saves other groups time and steers the search toward other routes.
plos-pone-0010214:
The authors were Carinne Piekema, Mark Rijpkema, Guillén Fernández, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used brain scans to separate two kinds of memory binding. Working memory must bind features into single items and items into sets. A brain region called the medial temporal lobe was thought to maintain those bound representations while we hold them in mind.

Building on earlier scan work, the team dissociated the brain activity for each binding type. Intra-item binding links features of one object, while inter-item binding links objects together. Showing separate neural support clarifies how short-term memory builds a coherent scene.
plos-pone-0010314:
The authors were Tanja Woyke, Damon Tighe, Konstantinos Mavromatis, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study sequenced a whole genome from one bacterial cell. Most finished microbial genomes came from bacteria grown in culture. Yet the vast majority of microbes refuse to grow in laboratories. Their genomes stayed out of reach for complete sequencing with standard methods.

Working from a single cell, the team recovered one complete genome. That proof opens the uncultured majority of microbial life to full genome study. Cataloging those hidden genomes can reshape understanding of ecosystems and evolution.
plos-pone-0009814:
Depo-Provera is a widely used hormone-based contraceptive shot. Meritxell Genescà and colleagues asked whether it weakens vaccine protection against SIV in female monkeys. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The monkeys had been immunized with an attenuated AIDS virus.

Attenuated means the vaccine virus was weakened so it could protect without causing disease. After treatment, the monkeys still held protection from an intravenous SIV challenge. That answer matters because contraceptive use is common where HIV risk is high. A vaccine that fails alongside contraception would be far less useful.
plos-pone-0009914:
Systematic reviews gather all evidence on a medical question, but evidence keeps growing. Chantelle Garritty and colleagues surveyed how review teams around the world keep reviews updated. Their international survey appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reviews guide treatment choices for millions of patients.

Updating a review means folding new studies into old conclusions. The survey asked teams when they update, how, and what blocks them. Outdated reviews can mislead doctors who trust them as current. The answers point to habits the whole field could adopt. The survey reached teams on several continents.
